ideas.title: Temperature on the winner: Heskes' energy-consistent winner and deterministic annealing (STVQ)
ideas.lens: statistical mechanics: free energy, phase transitions
ideas.what_it_changes: The winner line. Hard arm (Heskes): c = argmin_r E_r(x) with E_r(x) = sum_s h(r,s) d(x, w_s)^2 instead of argmin_r d(x, w_r). Soft arm (STVQ): responsibilities P(r|x) = exp(-beta E_r(x)) / sum_r' exp(-beta E_r'(x)), and the update of every unit s becomes w_s += alpha * [sum_r P(r|x) h(r,s)] * (x - w_s); beta rises on a schedule (annealing) so that the last passes are the hard Heskes map.
ideas.mechanism: Exact mapping. Erwin, Obermayer & Schulten (1992) showed the online SOM with the nearest-unit winner has no energy function in the continuum; Heskes (1999) showed that choosing the winner by the neighbourhood-weighted error restores one, so training becomes gradient descent on a definite cost and the fit/order trade-off becomes one function. Graepel, Burger & Obermayer (1997, 1998) put a temperature on the assignment: the free energy F = -(1/beta) sum_i log sum_r exp(-beta E_r(x_i)) has the SOM as its beta->infinity limit, and lowering the temperature passes through phase transitions at which the map unfolds dimension by dimension (the ordering phase as a physical transition rather than a wide radius). The failure of the plain SOM addressed: twists and folds frozen in by early hard assignments (TE 0.2 at small start radius in the metrics report) and the dependence of the end map on item order; soft responsibilities also move every unit a little, which starves fewer units. The project's own observation that an energy-free winner misleads (chaotic units: winner not nearest) is the negative image of this idea.
ideas.why_pd: Four PD classes with very different loudness and within-class spread after asinh; items near the corona / air-gap boundary flip winners under the hard rule from pass to pass, and the soft rule gives them split responsibility, which is also a usable output (a 'how sure' score per pulse for detection). No extra alignments: the DTW-SOM already computes DTW to all K units for the winner search, so E_r(x) and P(r|x) cost a K x K sum per item.
ideas.why_movement: Gestures with intermediate forms (a slow swipe vs a tap) get graded membership instead of a hard cell; the annealed assignment also tends to put the coarse gesture families in place before the fine differences, which is what a readable gesture map needs.
ideas.control: Online SOM / DTW-SOM with the identical seed, start and item order (the beta->infinity, nearest-winner limit of the same code); plus two radius-matched plain maps (start radius x1.5 and final radius 1) because a soft assignment blurs like a wider radius; plus a Langevin control (plain SOM with Gaussian noise of variance 2*alpha*T added to each update, T cooled on the same schedule as 1/beta) to show the gain is in the softness of the assignment, not in extra noise.
ideas.how_to_test: Data: all 12 benchmark sets (Euclidean arm) and the 8 series sets with DTW (soft arm with DTW responsibilities), pd_acoustic and the gesture / Wiimote sets as the headline. Map sizes 5x5, 8x8 and the project's 5*sqrt(N) rule, 10 seeds. Read QE and TE side by side, KL, TP, purity at equal used units, ARI/NMI, used units, alignments and seconds. Also record the energy F at the end of every pass (new column). Win = KL lower on most seeds at the same size AND QE not higher by more than the seed spread; a TE gain with QE loss is the CHAOSOM trade and does not count. Secondary win: lower seed-to-seed spread of QE and ARI (order independence).
ideas.cost: Implementation: 40 lines in the Rcpp loop (a K x K neighbourhood-error sum and a softmax in log-sum-exp form, fp64 is enough). Runtime: Euclidean +K^2 per item (about x1.5 on a 100-unit map); DTW arm essentially free (alignments already computed), except that LB_Keogh pruning of the winner search is lost in the soft arm because every unit needs its distance.
anchors: Heskes, T. (1999). Energy functions for self-organizing maps. In Oja & Kaski (eds), Kohonen Maps, Elsevier (from memory, unverified pages)
Graepel, T., Burger, M. & Obermayer, K. (1997). Phase transitions in stochastic self-organizing maps. Physical Review E 56(4), 3876-3890 (verified)
Graepel, T., Burger, M. & Obermayer, K. (1998). Self-organizing maps: generalizations and new optimization techniques. Neurocomputing 21, 19-30 (unverified)
Erwin, E., Obermayer, K. & Schulten, K. (1992). Self-organizing maps: ordering, convergence properties and energy functions. Biological Cybernetics 67, 47-55 (unverified)
Rose, K., Gurewitz, E. & Fox, G. C. (1990). Statistical mechanics and phase transitions in clustering. Physical Review Letters 65, 945-948 (unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no: the summary lists Heskes' winner as 'an early run, no result kept'; the annealed assignment was never tried. Related tested: CHAOSOM restarts (re-heating by radius) gave TE down, QE up, which is the trade this test must not repeat.
ideas.risk: A second annealing on top of the radius schedule may be redundant: the radius already does the ordering, and the soft assignment may simply act as extra radius (blur, QE up). On well-separated data (three blobs, pd noise class) the soft arm at moderate beta can pull units into the gaps. The energy F is not comparable across map sizes (falls with units, like QE).
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on TE/KL and on seed-to-seed stability; small on QE; unknown on ARI
ideas.problems: Not tested in the project (Heskes' winner: one early run, no result kept; annealed assignment never), so it clears check 1. The weak points are in the headroom and the control, not the mechanism. (a) The plain map's 'TE 0.2' failure exists only at a start radius of 0.5-1 (metrics report 4b); at the project's default start radius TE is about 0.03, so against the default control there is little order to win, and the proposer's win rule (KL lower at equal QE) will mostly measure noise. (b) With the default wide start radius h is nearly flat early (every E_r is a broad lattice average) and once the radius is below 1 the Heskes winner is the nearest winner again, so the hard arm acts only in a mid-training window. (c) The soft arm's update weight sum_r P(r|x) h(r,s) is a data-dependent convolution, i.e. a wider effective radius; the project already knows wider = blur (QE up), and the proposer's own risk section says so; a TE-for-QE trade is the CHAOSOM result in a new coat. (d) The 'how sure' per-pulse score is decorative: a softmax over distances from any hard-trained map gives it post hoc. (e) For the gesture sets the ARI is set by the DTW band (0.24 to 0.92 on CBF; Pebble flips the other way), not by twists, so expect nothing on ARI there. (f) The cost line is wrong for the hard arm too: E_r(x) needs d(x, w_s) for every s, so LB_Keogh pruning is lost in both arms, not only the soft one.
ideas.corrections: Run the hard arm first (a 5-line change) and make the sharp test the combination the project has been looking for: Heskes' winner with start radius x0.5 and x0.25 against the plain SOM / DTW-SOM at the same smaller radius AND the plain map at the default radius. The tearing lab showed the smaller start radius gives the fit gain at a small order cost; if the energy-consistent winner removes that order cost (Heskes' own point: kinks and twists are local minima of the energy), the pair beats the default on QE and TE together, which only the growing map has done. Report the energy F per pass only within one map size and schedule (it is not comparable across sizes, like QE). Soft arm and Langevin control only if the hard arm moves TE at the small radius. Reference detail: Heskes (1999) is pp. 303-315 of Kohonen Maps (verified); Erwin, Obermayer & Schulten (1992) Biol. Cybern. 67, 47-55 and Rose, Gurewitz & Fox (1990) PRL 65, 945 are correctly cited as far as I recall; Heskes & Kappen (1993, 'Error potentials for self-organization', ICNN) is the earlier source of the winner rule (unverified).

ideas.title: Soft-DTW as the free energy over alignment paths: update with the expected alignment
ideas.lens: statistical mechanics: log-partition function over paths
ideas.what_it_changes: The DTW-SOM's warp-before-update step. Instead of backtracking the single optimal path and averaging the series points matched to each prototype point, run the soft-DTW forward recursion (soft-min at temperature gamma) and its backward pass to get the expected alignment matrix E (sum over all paths of P(path) * indicator), then warp the series onto the prototype's axis with soft weights: x~_j = sum_i E_ij x_i / sum_i E_ij, and update w_j += alpha h (x~_j - w_j) as now. gamma anneals from about the median per-point cost down to 0, so the last passes are the exact DTW-SOM. Winner: keep hard DTW (cheap, keeps LB_Keogh) in arm A; soft-DTW divergence in arm B.
ideas.mechanism: Exact: soft-DTW_gamma(x,w) = -gamma log sum_paths exp(-cost(path)/gamma) is the free energy of a Boltzmann distribution over warping paths at temperature gamma, and its gradient with respect to the cost matrix is the expected path E (Cuturi & Blondel 2017). The failure addressed: the hard path is a single configuration; with ties and near-ties (the benchmark tests integer series full of ties) the chosen path jumps between neighbouring paths from update to update, so prototype points receive different series points each time and the prototype's timing jitters (the project's timing error, and the reason re-timing was needed). Averaging over near-optimal paths at a small gamma removes that jitter without changing which event is matched, and Cuturi & Blondel's barycentres are visibly smoother than DBA's, which the project found 'less ordered' in batch form.
ideas.why_pd: PD pulses are trigger-aligned, so the useful warping is small and local (ringing period, decay), exactly the regime of many near-equal paths where hard DTW is brittle; a 10% band over 125 samples at ringing periods of about 10-25 samples can also lock cycles onto the wrong cycle, and the soft path spreads that match. Honest: the project saw part of DTW's PD gain was in reading the map, not training it, so the gain here may be small.
ideas.why_movement: Gestures vary in speed within a gesture (the DTW territory where the growing DTW-SOM won: CBF, Wiimote shakes); prototypes read as 'the typical gesture' are the deliverable, and the soft path gives smoother, less jittery prototypes.
ideas.control: DTW-SOM (gamma = 0, same code path), same seed, start, order and window; plus the widening-window DTW-SOM (the project's other early-alignment smoother) so the two smoothing routes are compared; judge QE with hard DTW at the common window so no map is judged by its own distance.
ideas.how_to_test: Data: CBF at windows 10% and 20% (the ARI jump from 0.24 to 0.92 is the sensitivity to test), Trace, GunPoint, Synthetic Control, pd_acoustic, Wiimote shakes (different lengths, Section 4 of the growing report), solar I-V as the expected loser. Map sizes 5x5, 8x8, 5*sqrt(N); 10 seeds; gamma in {0, 0.1, 0.3, 1} x median per-point cost, annealed. Read QE (hard DTW), EV, TE, KL, TP, purity, ARI, NMI, used, timing error on CBF, alignments, seconds, and a new column: mean entropy of the alignment distribution per update. Win = timing error lower on most seeds with TE not higher, or QE lower on most seeds at the same TE; ARI on CBF 20% and the shakes.
ideas.cost: New C++ routine of about 120 lines (forward soft-min with log-sum-exp, backward pass for E, both banded). Runtime x2-3 per alignment in the update only; the winner search unchanged in arm A. Memory: one banded L x L matrix per alignment.
anchors: Cuturi, M. & Blondel, M. (2017). Soft-DTW: a differentiable loss function for time-series. ICML (unverified pages)
Blondel, M., Mensch, A. & Vert, J.-P. (2021). Differentiable divergences between time series. AISTATS (unverified)
Petitjean, F. et al. (2011). A global averaging method for dynamic time warping (DBA). Pattern Recognition 44(3) (unverified)
Somervuo, P. & Kohonen, T. (1999). Self-organizing maps and learning vector quantization for feature sequences. Neural Processing Letters 10 (unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no: soft-DTW is in the summary's never-tested list. Related tested: DTW in the update (helps), batch DBA (less ordered), re-timing (purity up, TE up), widening window (small gain for less work).
ideas.risk: gamma too large makes every point match every point, i.e. a Euclidean-like smeared average (the project's reason to leave the Kohonen SOM); gamma too small is the DTW-SOM to the last bit (a wash). The soft path is an average, not a path, so sharp edges (CBF cylinder) may blur: the opposite of what births-from-data achieved. Soft-DTW is not a metric and can be negative; keep reporting QE in hard DTW.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on timing error and QE for shapes that shift in time; small or none on order; unknown on PD
ideas.problems: On the summary's never-tested list, so new. Objections: (a) 'the benchmark tests integer series full of ties' is wrong for the series sets (UCR sets, CBF and asinh-scaled PD pressure are floats); near-ties, not ties, are the case, which weakens the jitter story. (b) The mechanism's known failure mode lands on exactly the two headline data sets: PD pulses ring at periods of 10-25 samples inside a 12-sample band, and the Wiimote shakes are oscillatory too; an expected path that spreads over two paths one cycle apart averages opposite phases, which is the Euclidean smearing the DTW-SOM exists to avoid. On non-oscillatory gestures (Pebble swings) and CBF it is harmless. (c) With gamma annealed to 0 the end state is the DTW-SOM, so the effect lives in the early passes, which is precisely what the widening window does (timing error 3.6 to 2.0, 28% fewer cells); the win must be over the widening window and the growing DTW-SOM (births from data, 3.6 to 2.0), not over the plain DTW-SOM, and the proposer includes only the first. (d) The timing error is defined on CBF only; for the gesture sets the deliverable is ARI, and the proposer's honest note that part of DTW's PD gain was in reading the map applies here too. (e) Soft-DTW responsibilities in arm B lose LB_Keogh; arm A keeps it, fine.
ideas.corrections: Keep arm A only (hard winner, soft path in the update). Controls: DTW-SOM, widening-window DTW-SOM and growing DTW-SOM, same seed, start, order and band; judge QE with hard DTW at the common band. Add two columns: the mean entropy of the alignment distribution per update (as proposed) and, for pd_acoustic and the shakes, the prototype's ringing amplitude relative to the mean amplitude of the series it wins, so that cycle averaging is visible rather than inferred. Choose gamma relative to the cost difference between the best and second-best paths (median over items), starting at 0.1x, since 'median per-point cost' is far too coarse for the oscillatory sets. Reference details from memory (unverified): Petitjean et al. (2011) is Pattern Recognition 44(3), 678-693; Somervuo & Kohonen (1999) is Neural Processing Letters 10(2), 151-159.

ideas.title: Magnification control: a density-dependent learning rate that sets how many units a class gets
ideas.lens: Fokker-Planck / density-matching (Ritter & Schulten), local learning (Bauer, Der & Herrmann)
ideas.what_it_changes: The learning-rate line. alpha_t becomes alpha_t * (p_hat(w_c))^m where p_hat(w_c) is a running estimate of the data density at the winner c (BDH use the winner's mean distance to the items it wins as an inverse density proxy; cheap, no new alignments). m sets the magnification exponent rho of the stationary prototype density q ~ p^rho: m = 0 is the plain SOM (rho = 2/3 in 1-D per Ritter & Schulten), a positive m moves toward rho = 1 (units proportional to data mass, equal usage, maximal entropy of the hit histogram), a negative m makes rare regions get MORE units (rho < 2/3, even rho < 0). From memory, BDH give rho = (2/3)(1+m) in 1-D, so m = 1/2 gives rho = 1 (unverified); check empirically from the hit histogram.
ideas.mechanism: Exact in 1-D (Ritter & Schulten's stationary-state / Fokker-Planck derivation gives the 2/3 law; Dersch & Tavan 1995 for finite neighbourhoods), approximate on 2-D lattices (Villmann & Claussen 2006 review). The plain SOM's failure: its prototype density follows p^(2/3), so dense compact classes are under-resolved and sparse loud classes eat the map; Ward's cut of the prototypes into as many groups as classes then splits a big class rather than separating the small one, which is one plausible reason ARI did not move with the growing map. Dead units are the extreme of the same law. The new diagnostic that comes with it: the empirical magnification exponent rho_hat, the slope of log(units per region) against log(local data density), reported per map.
ideas.why_pd: The four PD classes have a 4-decade loudness gap and, even after asinh, unequal within-class spread; the noise class is small and compact. For CLASSIFICATION set m toward rho = 1 so each class gets units in proportion to its 150 items. For DETECTION in deployment, where almost everything is ambient noise and PD pulses are rare, set m negative so the rare pulses get resolution instead of the noise cloud: a one-line knob for the base rate, which no other variant in the project offers.
ideas.why_movement: Activity streams are dominated by rest / walking; rare gestures are what matters. A negative magnification exponent gives rare gestures their own units; equal-usage (rho = 1) is the setting for balanced gesture sets.
ideas.control: Online SOM / DTW-SOM (m = 0); DeSieno's conscience (bias the winner choice by win frequency, b_r = C(1/K - f_r)) as the cheap rival that equalises usage without a density estimate; k-means usage as the fit ceiling. Compare purity only at equal used units (purity rises with units, the metrics report's trap).
ideas.how_to_test: Data: pd_acoustic (balanced, 150 each) and a deliberately imbalanced pd_acoustic (e.g. 600 noise, 50 of each PD class, resampled per seed) for the detection setting; the gesture sets with a rare class held at 5%; colours as the sanity set (12 families). Map sizes 5x5, 8x8, 5*sqrt(N); m in {-1, -0.5, 0, 0.25, 0.5}; 10 seeds. Read used units, entropy of the hit histogram and rho_hat (new columns), QE, EV, TE, KL, TP, purity at equal used, ARI, NMI, and for detection the per-class recall from the Ward cut. Win = ARI/NMI higher on most seeds at the same map size with QE not worse by more than the seed spread (rho = 1 arm), and rare-class recall higher on most seeds (negative-m arm). A used-units gain alone does not count (the project's long-run-mean control already rescues dead units without any other gain).
ideas.cost: Implementation: 15 lines (a per-unit running mean of winner distance; one multiplication). Runtime: none measurable.
anchors: Ritter, H. & Schulten, K. (1986). On the stationary state of Kohonen's self-organizing sensory mapping. Biological Cybernetics 54, 99-106 (unverified)
Bauer, H.-U., Der, R. & Herrmann, M. (1996). Controlling the magnification factor of self-organizing feature maps. Neural Computation 8, 757-771 (verified)
Villmann, T. & Claussen, J. C. (2006). Magnification control in self-organizing maps and neural gas. Neural Computation 18(2), 446-469 (verified)
Dersch, D. R. & Tavan, P. (1995). Asymptotic level density in topological feature maps. IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks 6(1), 230-236 (unverified)
DeSieno, D. (1988). Adding a conscience to competitive learning. IEEE ICNN (unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no. Related tested: dead units rescued by the long-run mean output (no gain where no unit is dead), chaotic units (fewer used units, worse map), growing map births where the error is largest (a usage-driven growth, which did not move ARI).
ideas.risk: The online density proxy is noisy and m > 0 amplifies the learning rate in dense regions, which can destabilise the late passes; on asinh-scaled PD the within-class spreads may already be close enough that rho hardly matters; on 2-D hex lattices the exponent is only approximately controllable. The rival (conscience) may do the same job for free.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on used units and ARI/NMI where classes have unequal spread; large on rare-class recall in the detection setting if the base rate is the issue; none on TE
ideas.problems: Not tested; the nearest relative is a draft ('newborn units learn faster', a per-unit learning-rate boost) that gave no gain, and the long-run-mean rescue of dead units. Objections: (a) The density proxy is not BDH's: Bauer, Der & Herrmann estimate the local density from the spacing of the winner's prototype to its lattice neighbours (raised to the data dimension); a winner's mean distance to the items it wins is a within-unit spread, which on series data of unknown intrinsic dimension conflates spread with density, so m no longer maps to rho and the quoted rho = (2/3)(1+m) (consistent with the 1-D result as I recall it, unverified) does not apply. (b) With negative m the factor p_hat^m explodes in sparse regions: a unit that wins one far item gets a rate above 1; it must be clipped, and the clip is a second knob. (c) The claim that unequal magnification is why ARI did not move is a hypothesis the cached maps can test at zero cost: count units per class on the pd_acoustic and gesture maps; with balanced sets (150 per PD class) and asinh scaling the units may already be near proportional, and then the Ward cut cannot be moved by any m. (d) DeSieno's conscience drives usage to rho = 1; it is a rival for the m > 0 arm only; for the negative-m arm the rival is the plain SOM itself (rho = 2/3 already over-represents sparse regions relative to mass) and there is no cheap rival, which the proposer should say. (e) The movement claim about rest/walking-dominated streams is about continuous activity data; the project's gesture sets are segmented and balanced, so the rare-gesture arm needs a constructed imbalance, as proposed, and is then a synthetic claim until real streams exist.
ideas.corrections: Do the zero-cost diagnostic first (units per class and the hit-histogram entropy on the cached benchmark maps for pd_acoustic, Pebble, Wiimote); only if a large class holds disproportionately many units is the rho = 1 arm worth running. Use BDH's own estimate (prototype spacing to lattice neighbours, in the chosen distance, exponent absorbed into m) or, simpler and exact in spirit, the winner's running hit frequency f_r with alpha_r = alpha (K f_r)^m, which makes m = 0 the plain SOM and makes the conscience the natural m > 0 rival; clip alpha_r to at most alpha. Report rho_hat as the slope of log(units per class) on log(class mass) across the resampled imbalance levels rather than a local density regression, which is ill-posed on series. For the detection arm the honest control is the plain SOM on the same imbalanced resample plus per-class recall from the Ward cut, exactly as proposed. Anchors: BDH (1996) Neural Computation 8, 757-771 verified; Villmann & Claussen (2006) and Ritter & Schulten (1986) correctly cited as far as I recall.

ideas.title: Renormalisation in time and in the map: train the envelope first, the ringing later; tree-structured winner search
ideas.what_it_changes: Two loops. (a) Time: the first passes train on series downsampled 4x (125 -> 32 points; for PD, the asinh of the Hilbert envelope plus a 4x-decimated signal), with prototypes at that resolution; at a set pass prototypes are upsampled (linear, or the DTW path projected as in FastDTW) and training continues at full resolution with the band restricted to a corridor around the coarse alignment. (b) Map: the winner search descends a tree of coarse maps (TS-SOM: a 2x2, then 4x4, then the full map, each level initialised from its parent), searching only the children of the best parent and its neighbours; the growing map's births can be read as the same hierarchy built one unit at a time.
ideas.mechanism: Mostly a metaphor, with one exact piece: block-averaging in time is a renormalisation step, and the DTW path at the coarse level bounds the fine path (FastDTW's projection), so the fine alignments cost O(L x corridor) instead of O(L x band). The failure addressed: the DTW-SOM's cost (3-15x the classic SOM in the growing report) and the fact that early, wide-radius passes order the map by gross shape anyway, so computing fine alignments there is wasted; the project's own widening window and growing map are partial versions of this (window annealing and map annealing); the time axis is the missing third. The tree search is the known approximation that can miss the true winner, which the chaotic-units report showed is harmful if frequent, so the missed-winner rate must be reported.
ideas.why_pd: The physics of a PD pulse separates by scale: the envelope (amplitude, decay time, the 4-decade loudness) is the coarse level and the ringing frequency the fine level, so coarse-first training orders the map by the physically primary quantities and refines by ringing afterwards. 500 kS/s with ringing periods of 10-25 samples means the plain 4x decimation aliases, so the envelope is the right coarse representation, not decimation alone.
ideas.why_movement: A gesture's gross trajectory at 4x decimation is what separates gesture classes; tremor and fine timing come later. Also the practical reason: accelerometer series of hundreds of points make DTW-SOM training slow, and alignments are the cost the project counts.
ideas.control: Plain DTW-SOM at full resolution (same seed, start, order); plain DTW-SOM with the same number of DTW cells as the multi-scale run (a compute-matched control, e.g. fewer passes or a narrower band); the widening-window DTW-SOM; the growing DTW-SOM; for the tree search, the exact winner search with LB_Keogh.
ideas.how_to_test: Data: the 8 series sets, pd_acoustic with envelope coarse level, Wiimote shakes; map sizes 5x5, 8x8, 5*sqrt(N); switch to full resolution at 30%, 50%, 70% of training; 10 seeds. Read QE (hard DTW at full resolution), EV, TE, KL, TP, purity, ARI, NMI, used, timing error on CBF, DTW cells and alignments, seconds, and the missed-winner rate for the tree search. Win = same QE/TE/KL as the full-resolution DTW-SOM within the seed spread at under half the DTW cells, or better TE at equal cells; for the tree search, the same winners in over 98% of steps at O(log K) alignments.
ideas.cost: Implementation: 100 lines (decimation/envelope, prototype upsampling, corridor band, level-wise tree). Runtime: the point of the idea; expected 2-5x fewer DTW cells overall.
anchors: Koikkalainen, P. & Oja, E. (1990). Self-organizing hierarchical feature maps. IJCNN San Diego, 279-284 (verified)
Salvador, S. & Chan, P. (2007). Toward accurate dynamic time warping in linear time and space. Intelligent Data Analysis 11(5), 561-580 (unverified)
Luttrell, S. P. (1989). Hierarchical self-organising networks. IEE ICANN (unverified)
ideas.already_tested: partly: widening window (helps, 28% fewer DTW cells), growing map (17% fewer alignments), skipping far units (11-15% fewer alignments, little time saved), LB_Keogh (half the alignments, same winners). Not tested: coarse-to-fine in time, corridor bands from a coarse path, a tree-structured winner search.
ideas.risk: Quality may not move at all (then it is a speed-up, which the project values but files separately); the upsampling step can blur sharp prototypes; the tree search's missed winners are a known harm; aliasing of PD ringing if decimation is used without the envelope.
ideas.expected_gain: large on alignments and seconds; small or none on QE/TE; unknown on ARI
ideas.problems: Partly tested (widening window, growing map, LB_Keogh, skipping far units) and the proposer says so; coarse-to-fine in time is new. Objections: (a) It is a bundle. The tree search is redundant with LB_Keogh at K <= 100 (exact winners, half the alignments) and reintroduces missed winners; the chaotic report showed wrong winners harm when far from the nearest unit (median hops above random), and a tree search's misses are near misses, so the harm is smaller than the proposer fears but the gain is also small: once the radius is below ~1.5 most alignments are in the update to the neighbourhood, not in the winner search (skipping far units saved only 11-15% of alignments and a tenth of the time), so O(log K) winner alignments buys little. (b) 4x decimation aliases PD ringing (periods 10-25 samples become 2.5-6; anything under 8 aliases without a filter); the envelope is the right coarse level, but then the envelope is a different representation, and with a 4-decade loudness gap plus decay times the envelope alone may carry nearly all the class information, which would make the fine level pointless for PD and is itself a finding worth having. (c) After the switch the remaining passes have alpha <= 0.25 and radius <= 1.5, so blurred upsampled prototypes may never sharpen; the proposed win rule (same QE/TE/KL within the seed spread at half the cells) is honest about that. (d) For gestures (Wiimote 41-385 points, Pebble 100-455) 4x decimation is standard practice and gives about 16x fewer DTW cells, so a speed-up is near certain, but the project files speed-ups separately and the ARI is set by the band.
ideas.corrections: Split and shrink: drop the tree search; test coarse-to-fine in time alone as a speed-up with the compute-matched control (plain DTW-SOM with the same number of DTW cells via fewer passes or a narrower band) and the widening window. Add the envelope-only online SOM and DTW-SOM on pd_acoustic as controls (ARI, purity) so the report says whether ringing carries class information at all; if it does not, that is the PD result and the multi-scale map is moot there. At the fine level use the FastDTW corridor (coarse path projected, radius 1-2) rather than the full band, and count DTW cells, not alignments, since the cells are what the idea saves. On the growing DTW-SOM births at the coarse level are coarse medoids, upsampled at the switch. Anchors: Koikkalainen & Oja (1990) is the TS-SOM paper; Salvador & Chan (2007) Intelligent Data Analysis 11(5), 561-580 is right as far as I recall.

ideas.title: Manhattan (L1) and Huber local costs: the median map
ideas.lens: distances and alignments inside the SOM
ideas.what_it_changes: The local cost in both the winner search and the update: |x_j - m_j| (or Huber: quadratic below delta, linear above) instead of (x_j - m_j)^2, in the Euclidean SOM and as the per-cell cost inside the DTW recursion. The update becomes the gradient of that cost: m_j += alpha*h*clip(x_j - m_j, +-delta) for Huber, or alpha*h*s*sign(x_j - m_j) for pure L1 (s a step scale such as the data's median absolute deviation); along a DTW path each prototype point moves towards the MEDIAN (not the mean) of its matched series points.
ideas.mechanism: The squared cost lets one far-off sample (a spike, a glitch, a late ringing cycle the band could not align) dominate both the choice of winner and the pull on the prototype: the mean is dragged and the prototype smears. The minimiser of an L1 cost is the median, which does not care how far an outlier sits. Huber keeps the plain step for ordinary residuals (so the map stays close to the control) and caps the pull of large ones. Failure addressed: online SOM prototypes are averages that a few extreme items bend, and the grey/dead units on noisy sets.
ideas.why_pd: After asinh the loud pulses still have a few extreme samples in their first cycles; with squared cost those cycles decide everything and the decay tail, which separates a void discharge from an air-gap one, is drowned. L1 gives the tail a vote proportional to its number of samples, not their square, and is robust to the occasional clipped or doubly-triggered pulse. The noise class, small everywhere, stops being pulled towards whichever loud unit it happens to be nearest.
ideas.why_movement: Accelerometer series carry impacts and sensor spikes that are not part of the gesture; L1/Huber stops a single impact from choosing the winner. Little effect on smooth data such as GunPoint.
ideas.control: The same online SOM / DTW-SOM with squared cost, same start, same order of items, same schedule. delta -> infinity must give the control to the last bit (the correctness check).
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic, GunPoint, GesturePebbleZ1, ShakeGestureWiimoteZ; map sizes 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds; delta in {0.5, 1, 2} x the median absolute residual of the control at the end of training, plus pure L1. Read ARI, NMI, purity (classes), TE, KL (order), used units, seconds; QE judged in L2 for all maps (QE in L1 only among the L1 maps). A win: ARI higher and TE not higher on >= 7 of 10 seeds at every size; a wash if the medians differ by less than the seed spread.
ideas.cost: One line in the local cost and one in the step; the DTW recursion keeps its size; the median along the path is a small sort per prototype point (negligible at 125 points).
anchors: Huber (1964) Ann. Math. Statist. 35, 73-101
Kohonen & Somervuo (1998) Neurocomputing 21, 19-30: median SOM / batch map with generalised medians
Kohonen (2001) Self-Organizing Maps, 3rd ed. (Minkowski/L1 remark; page unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no: the project's cost is squared everywhere; the only median it uses is the DTW medoid at births in the growing map.
ideas.risk: Pure L1's sign step has constant size, so late in training the prototype oscillates +-s around the item unless s follows the learning rate; Huber avoids this. On smooth data the Huber map equals the control at most steps -> wash. The QE trap: an L1 map must not be judged by L2 QE alone.
ideas.expected_gain: small to moderate on pd_acoustic noise-class purity and used units; small elsewhere; a robustness gain more than an accuracy gain.
ideas.problems: The premise is borrowed from the raw-pressure picture, but the project trains on asinh(p / 1 mPa): the four decades of loudness collapse to a 0-10 range and a tail at a tenth of the peak sits only ln(10) = 2.3 units below it, so the squared cost no longer lets 'the loud early cycles decide everything' - asinh has already done most of the robustification L1 claims. The 'grey/dead units on noisy sets' failure is the chaotic-units failure (Section 2 of the summary), not something the plain SOM shows on pd_acoustic. Along a DTW path most prototype points receive one or two series points, where the median equals the mean, so the median-along-path change is cosmetic. Pure L1's sign step oscillates (admitted). What Huber actually does on asinh data is cap the loud-vs-quiet residuals, i.e. it quietly down-weights loudness, which is the same effect L3 gives with a readable knob. The case where Huber genuinely helps, doubly-triggered or clipped pulses, is rare in this lab set (150 of 1000 waveforms, fixed source, anechoic chamber) and matters in the field.
ideas.corrections: Keep Huber only; treat pure L1 as the delta -> 0 end and report it, do not tune it. Add the chaotic-units report's diagnostic: the share of steps where the Huber winner differs from the squared-cost winner; below a few percent the result is a wash by construction. Tie delta to the running median residual (so it follows the learning rate), not to a fixed multiple of the end-of-training residual of the control. Add a stress test that matches the robustness claim: splice a second pulse or a clipped peak into 10% of the items and read purity of the noise and corona units. Present it as the cheap first probe of the loudness question, read next to L3's lambda sweep. Anchors are fine: Huber 1964 Ann. Math. Statist. 35:73-101 and Kohonen & Somervuo 1998 Neurocomputing 21:19-30 (generalised medians) verified; the Minkowski remark in Kohonen 2001 is plausible (Section 1.2 of the book, unverified page).

ideas.title: Cosine / correlation distance with a separate loudness coordinate: shape plus loudness split
ideas.lens: distances and alignments inside the SOM
ideas.what_it_changes: The distance becomes 1 - corr(x, m) (correlation = cosine of the centred series) on the shape, plus lambda*(l_x - l_m)^2 on a scalar loudness coordinate l = log RMS of the raw pressure (or of the raw acceleration). Update: Kohonen's dot-product rule m <- (m + alpha*h*x_hat) / ||m + alpha*h*x_hat|| with x_hat the centred unit-norm series, so the prototype stays on the unit sphere; the ordinary step for l_m. With DTW the warped cousin is z-normalised DTW (already tested).
ideas.mechanism: Euclidean distance mixes amplitude and shape: two pulses of the same shape at 10x loudness are far apart, two pulses of different ringing frequency but the same energy may be close. Splitting shape (scale-free) from loudness (one number with its own weight) makes the map's axes readable and lets lambda say how much loudness counts. Failure addressed: the SOM on asinh series organises largely by loudness, so classes that differ in shape but overlap in loudness share a region.
ideas.why_pd: Loudness spans four decades and IS a class cue (corona quiet, air gap loud); a pure shape distance would throw away the best cue, which is why z-normalised DTW gained nothing. The split keeps it as one coordinate. lambda -> inf is a loudness-only map, a 1-D control that tells how much of the ARI is loudness alone, a number the project does not yet have; lambda = 0 is shape only.
ideas.why_movement: Gesture size varies by person; correlation removes size and offset per channel, the loudness coordinate keeps vigour (running vs walking in BasicMotions is largely a magnitude difference). For multi-channel data sum the per-channel correlations.
ideas.control: The Euclidean SOM on the asinh series (same seeds); the loudness-only map (lambda -> inf) and the shape-only map (lambda = 0) as the two ends; z-normalised DTW-SOM for the warped case.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic and BasicMotions/UWaveGestureLibrary; sizes 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds; lambda in {0, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, inf} chosen on seeds 11-15, tested on seeds 1-10 (as the project did for mending). Read ARI, NMI, purity, used units, TE and KL within the same distance, the loudness-only ARI. Win: ARI above both ends and above the Euclidean control on >= 7 of 10 seeds.
ideas.cost: Cheap: dot products; one extra coordinate; the sphere projection is one line.
anchors: Kohonen (2001) Self-Organizing Maps, 3rd ed.: the dot-product (scalar-product) SOM (section unverified)
Paparrizos & Gravano (2015) SIGMOD 1855-1870: correlation as the shape view
ideas.already_tested: partly: z-normalised DTW (shape only, warped, raw values averaged) gave no gain in general and one win on the solar I-V curves; no loudness coordinate and no sphere update were tested.
ideas.risk: lambda is a knob; the correlation of a noise series with anything is near 0, so noise items may scatter over many units (purity down) unless the loudness coordinate catches them; centring removes the DC level, which on PD is meaningful only for the noise class.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on PD readability and on knowing what loudness alone gives; small to moderate on ARI.
ideas.problems: On asinh data the Euclidean SOM already mixes shape with log-loudness, so lambda re-parametrises something the control has implicitly; the gain, if any, comes from making loudness one coordinate rather than 125. The shape-only end is phase-sensitive: a quarter-cycle trigger jitter (3 samples at a 40 kHz ringing, 500 kS/s) makes two identical pulses nearly uncorrelated, so without a shift in front of it the correlation distance can be worse than Euclidean on the ringing classes. Noise items are equidistant from every unit under correlation (corr = 0 +- 1/sqrt(125) = 0.09) and scatter unless loudness catches them (admitted). The lambda -> inf control is a 1-D SOM on one number; fine, but it is a histogram of log RMS. z-normalised DTW, the warped cousin, was tested and gave no general gain, which the author notes.
ideas.corrections: Compute the correlation after the best global shift within +-5% (fold L6: this is k-Shape's SBD with a loudness coordinate). Define loudness on the raw pressure (log10 RMS or log10 peak), not on the asinh series. The correlation SOM equals the Euclidean SOM on z-normalised series plus a renormalisation after each update; check that with renormalisation off it reproduces the project's SOM on z-scored inputs bit for bit. The PD-engineering reason this experiment is worth running: in the lab the microphone distance and the sources are fixed, so loudness is partly a geometry artefact that will not transfer to a substation; the lambda = 0 ARI is the transferable part, the lambda -> inf ARI is the artefact - report both ends as the finding, whatever the middle does. For movement, sum per-channel correlations only after L8's per-channel z-scaling over the data set. Anchors: Paparrizos & Gravano 2015 SIGMOD 1855-1870 verified; Kohonen's dot-product SOM is in the book (Section 3.4 region, unverified).

ideas.title: Soft-DTW with its smooth barycentre as the update
ideas.lens: distances and alignments inside the SOM
ideas.what_it_changes: DTW's hard min is replaced by a soft-min with temperature gamma in the winner search (soft-DTW_gamma) and in the update: m <- m - alpha*h*grad_m softDTW_gamma(x, m), computed by the backward pass (the expected-alignment matrix E), so prototype point j moves towards a weighted mean of ALL series points with weights E_ij, not only the points on one best path. gamma -> 0 reproduces the project's along-path update to the last bit.
ideas.mechanism: With ringing, many alignments are near-ties (cycle i of the series matches cycle j or j+-1 of the prototype at almost the same cost); hard DTW picks one arbitrarily and the update follows it, so successive items pull the prototype towards different cycle pairings and its ringing is smeared or pinched (the 'events bunch in the middle' the project saw). Soft-DTW averages over the near-ties, so the pull is consistent from item to item, and the cost is differentiable in m: the online SOM becomes a true gradient descent for DTW, as it already is for Euclidean.
ideas.why_pd: Exactly the ringing phase-slip case: the smooth barycentre should give prototypes whose ringing frequency is the class's, not a compromise between pairings.
ideas.why_movement: Repeated strokes (a wave, a shake) create the same near-ties; works unchanged with dependent multivariate DTW and one gamma.
ideas.control: The project's DTW-SOM (hard path, same band, same seeds, same start and order); the gamma -> 0 map must equal it bit for bit. A cheaper middle option, hard winner + soft update, is a second contender.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic, CBF at window 20%, GesturePebbleZ1, ShakeGestureWiimoteZ; sizes 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds; gamma in {0.01, 0.1, 1} x the median local cost. Judge QE in HARD DTW for all maps (soft-DTW values can be negative and depend on gamma); TE and KL in hard DTW; ARI, NMI, purity; timing error on CBF; seconds and cells computed (forward + backward = 2x). Win: QE (hard DTW) and TE both lower on >= 7 of 10 seeds, or ARI up with TE not up.
ideas.cost: Forward + backward pass per alignment, about 2-3x the DTW time; the L x w matrix is kept (trivial at 125 points); about 150 lines of C++.
anchors: Cuturi & Blondel (2017) ICML, PMLR 70, 894-903: soft-DTW and its barycentre
Petitjean, Ketterlin & Gancarski (2011) Pattern Recognition 44(3), 678-693: DBA, already in the project
ideas.already_tested: no: listed as untested in the summary report.
ideas.risk: The smooth barycentre blurs sharp edges (the project saw linear interpolation blur edges when re-timing during training); too large a gamma turns the map into a Euclidean SOM with a band; the soft winner can differ from the hard winner, which complicates the comparison with the control.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on PD and other ringing-like data (phase consistency of prototypes, TE); small on smooth data.
ideas.problems: (1) 'gamma -> 0 reproduces the project's along-path update to the last bit' is wrong as written: the soft-DTW gradient with respect to m_j is sum_i E_ij * 2(m_j - x_i), the SUM over matched points, whereas the project moves m_j towards the along-path MEAN; at gamma -> 0 the gradient step is n_j times the project's step for a point matched to n_j series points - exactly the pinched points. Log-sum-exp at tiny gamma is also not bit-exact. (2) The soft winner is a different winner, so winner and update change together and the comparison with the control is confounded; only 'hard winner + soft update' is a clean contender. (3) 'Exactly the ringing phase-slip case' is decorative without a diagnostic: with a 12-sample band and a ringing period of about 12 samples, a one-cycle slip sits at the band edge, so near-ties may be rare. (4) Soft-DTW barycentres blur sharp onsets, and the onset is the one PD feature that must not blur. (5) The 'events bunch in the middle' finding is real (summary, timing error 4.4 vs 0.8) but the project attributes it to free runs of copied points, which L9 targets more directly.
ideas.corrections: Normalise E column-wise (a soft along-path mean) so that gamma -> 0 gives the project's update within floating-point tolerance, and claim 'within 1e-9', not 'bit for bit'. Run a pre-test before writing 150 lines: on a trained hard DTW-SOM compute E at gamma = 0.1 x median local cost and the share of prototype points whose E mass is split over two or more ringing cycles; below about 10% skip the experiment. Keep the hard winner; judge QE, TE, KL in hard DTW; add the CBF timing error and a PD onset-sharpness reading (prototype rise time against its class median). Cuturi & Blondel 2017 ICML PMLR 70:894-903 and Petitjean et al. 2011 Pattern Recognition 44(3):678-693 verified.

ideas.title: Shape-based distance (k-Shape): one global shift, nothing elastic
ideas.lens: distances and alignments inside the SOM
ideas.what_it_changes: The alignment becomes one global shift s* = argmax_s crosscorr(x, m)(s), found by FFT in O(L log L) or directly over +-max shift; the distance is the Euclidean (or L1) distance after shifting x by s* (amplitude kept), or 1 - NCCc, k-Shape's z-normalised version. The update shifts the series by s* and applies the plain point-by-point step (zero-padded ends); the batch analogue is k-Shape's shape extraction (top eigenvector of the aligned centred members).
ideas.mechanism: DTW buys shift invariance together with an elastic freedom it does not need: within a 10% band it can compress or stretch a ringing cycle and make two pulses of different ringing frequency look alike, and the ringing frequency IS the class cue. One global shift removes trigger jitter (a few samples) and nothing else, so frequency and decay stay in the distance. Failure addressed on both sides: the Euclidean SOM smears onsets through jitter, the DTW-SOM warps frequency away.
ideas.why_pd: Pulses are triggered by the current pulse, so the only misalignment is the acoustic onset jitter (propagation and trigger delay): a global shift is the physically right invariance; with the un-normalised version the 4-decade loudness stays in the distance.
ideas.why_movement: Start-time jitter yes, tempo variation no: expect SBD close to Euclidean on gestures that differ in speed; useful as a cheap first alignment before DTW with a small band.
ideas.control: Euclidean SOM (shift 0) and DTW-SOM (band 10%), same seeds; the DTW-SOM with a tiny band (2% of L) is the nearest rival and the decisive control; every map also mapped and clustered with each distance (the project's 'read with DTW' check).
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic above all; also CBF and GunPoint; sizes 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds; max shift in {5%, 10%, 20%} of L. Read ARI, NMI, purity, used units, TE and KL (own distance and Euclidean), QE in Euclidean after the best shift, seconds, number of cross-correlations vs DTW cells. Win: ARI >= the DTW-SOM's and TE <= on >= 7 of 10 seeds at a fraction of the alignments.
ideas.cost: Far cheaper than DTW: O(L log L) per comparison; about 60 lines with an FFT or a direct correlation over the allowed shifts.
anchors: Paparrizos & Gravano (2015) SIGMOD, 1855-1870: k-Shape, SBD, shape extraction
Paparrizos & Gravano (2017) ACM TODS (extended version; issue unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no: listed as untested ('a shape-based distance, one global shift').
ideas.risk: On CBF-like data with stretched events SBD loses to DTW by design; zero-padded ends leave the prototype's edges updated by fewer items (edge fading); the z-normalised NCCc throws away loudness (use the un-normalised version or the loudness split of idea 3).
ideas.expected_gain: moderate to large on PD (honest guess: the strongest single idea for the pulses); small on gestures.
ideas.problems: The physics is right for THIS data set: fixed geometry, anechoic chamber, current-pulse trigger, so the only misalignment is acoustic propagation and trigger jitter of a few samples (1 degree C moves the speed of sound by 0.6 m/s, about 1.5 us = 0.8 samples over 30 cm; streamer-path variation a few us). But that also means the gain over the tiny-band DTW-SOM and the plain Euclidean SOM may be nil: the project already found the Euclidean SOM read with DTW close to the DTW-SOM on pd_acoustic, so alignment is not where the PD gain lives. 'The strongest single idea for the pulses' is overclaimed; the strongest is the representation (L11) with this shift in front of it. On CBF it loses by design (admitted). The un-normalised cross-correlation is set by the loudest cycles, which is what we want here. Zero-padded edge fading is minor with asinh tails near zero.
ideas.corrections: State the likely outcome honestly: 'SBD = tiny-band DTW = Euclidean on pd_acoustic' is the probable and still informative result, pointing to L11. Test max shift +-2% and +-5% (8 samples), not 20%. Add the diagnostic 'distribution of s* per class on the trained map': if it stays within +-2 samples for every class, the physics says drop the elastic family on PD altogether. Use SBD as the alignment inside L3 (shift, then correlate) and L11 (shift, then envelope or spectrum). The k-Shape eigenvector shape extraction is the batch analogue and is not needed for the online map. Paparrizos & Gravano 2015 SIGMOD 1855-1870 verified; the 2017 extended version is ACM TODS 42(2) article 8 (plausible).

ideas.title: Elastic measures with a priced warp: TWED, MSM, ERP, LCSS
ideas.lens: distances and alignments inside the SOM
ideas.what_it_changes: The DTW recursion gets an explicit price for warping: TWED adds nu*|t_i - t_j| for every matched pair and lambda for every deletion (stiffness nu); MSM charges c for each move/split/merge; ERP charges |x_i - g| for a gap; LCSS counts matches within epsilon. The update keeps the project's rule: backtrack the optimal alignment, matched pairs pull the prototype point towards the series point, deleted or gapped points leave the prototype point alone (ERP: a pull towards g), LCSS moves only matched points.
ideas.mechanism: The Sakoe-Chiba band is a cliff: warping inside it is free, outside forbidden. A soft growing penalty lets small jitter through, makes a one-cycle stretch expensive and a three-cycle stretch very expensive, so the measure prefers the diagonal. Failure addressed: the band sensitivity the project found (CBF ARI 0.24 at 10% vs 0.92 at 20%, solar I-V better at 5%); a penalty may make the result less brittle than a hard band, and it is the cleaner form of the 'weighted DTW' the summary lists as untested.
ideas.why_pd: The frequency-vs-jitter argument of idea 6, kept elastic: jitter free, cycle compression costly, decay-rate differences allowed.
ideas.why_movement: Tempo variation within a gesture is gradual, so a penalty proportional to |t_i - t_j| matches human motion better than a free band; LCSS's epsilon makes sensor glitches not count.
ideas.control: The DTW-SOM with the same band (the penalised measures keep the band so that the band is not the confound); nu -> 0, lambda -> 0 (or c -> 0) must reproduce the DTW-SOM to the last bit.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic; CBF at 10% and 20%; pv_iv at 5% and 10%; GesturePebbleZ1; ShakeGestureWiimoteZ; sizes 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds; TWED nu in {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1} x median local cost per time step, lambda in {0, 0.5, 1}; MSM c in {0.01, 0.1, 1}. Judge QE in plain DTW for all; TE, KL; ARI, NMI, purity; timing error on CBF; and the brittleness: the spread of ARI across bands (a flatter band curve is also a win). Win: ARI and TE better than the DTW-SOM at the DTW-SOM's best band on >= 7 of 10 seeds.
ideas.cost: The same O(L*w) recursion with one or two extra terms per cell; TWED needs time stamps (trivial); about 100 lines of C++ per measure.
anchors: Marteau (2009) IEEE TPAMI 31(2), 306-318: TWED
Stefan, Athitsos & Das (2013) IEEE TKDE 25(6), 1425-1438: MSM
Chen & Ng (2004) VLDB: ERP
Vlachos, Kollios & Gunopulos (2002) ICDE: LCSS
Jeong, Jeong & Omitaomu (2011) Pattern Recognition 44(9), 2231-2240: weighted DTW
Lines & Bagnall (2015) DMKD 29(3), 565-592: elastic ensemble; the measures' 1-NN accuracies differ little
ideas.already_tested: partly: the hard band (window width) was swept and found data-dependent; length-normalised DTW was tested (a trade, not a fix); no soft warping penalty and no edit-style gaps were tested.
ideas.risk: In 1-NN classification the elastic measures differ by a few percent (Lines & Bagnall 2015), so the gain in a SOM may be as small; two more knobs; LCSS is not a metric and its distance saturates, giving flat QE and dead units.
ideas.expected_gain: small to moderate; the valuable output is the band-brittleness curve per measure.
ideas.problems: Four measures x 3-4 knobs each x 6 data sets x 3 sizes x 10 seeds is a grid, not an experiment, and Lines & Bagnall 2015 already say the measures differ by a few percent in 1-NN; the author expects a 'small' gain and sells the band-brittleness curve as the output. TWED, MSM, ERP and LCSS bring edit semantics (deletions, gaps) with no counterpart in the project's along-path update and no PD motivation - a PD pulse has nothing to delete; LCSS saturates (admitted). For PD the priced warp competes with L6, whose physics says no elastic freedom at all is the right prior, so the PD line is decorative. The claim 'nu -> 0, lambda -> 0 reproduces the DTW-SOM to the last bit' is wrong for TWED: its match cost includes |x_{i-1} - m_{j-1}| and its recursion differs from DTW's even at zero stiffness.
ideas.corrections: Reduce to the one-knob version that is already on the project's untested list: weighted DTW (Jeong, Jeong & Omitaomu 2011 Pattern Recognition 44(9):2231-2240), a logistic weight on |i - j| multiplying the local cost. g = 0 reproduces the DTW-SOM bit for bit, the update is unchanged, and 'does a priced warp flatten the band curve?' is answered with one parameter on CBF at 10%/20% and pv_iv at 5%/10%, where the brittleness was measured. Only if the curve flattens consider TWED (Marteau 2009 TPAMI 31(2):306-318 verified). Drop ERP, MSM and LCSS. Stefan et al. 2013 TKDE 25(6):1425-1438, Chen & Ng 2004 VLDB, Vlachos et al. 2002 ICDE, Lines & Bagnall 2015 DMKD 29(3):565-592 all correctly attributed.

ideas.title: Multi-channel series: dependent vs independent DTW and the channel-locked update
ideas.lens: distances and alignments inside the SOM
ideas.what_it_changes: For c-channel series DTW_D uses one path with local cost sum_c (x_ic - m_jc)^2 (one alignment per comparison); DTW_I aligns each channel separately and sums. Update: DTW_D moves all channels of prototype point j towards the matched series point, so the prototype remains one consistent motion; DTW_I gives each channel its own path and its own along-path mean. Channel weights w_c (per-channel z-scaling, or relevance weights) enter the local cost and the step.
ideas.mechanism: A gesture is one motion seen by 3-6 channels that share one time axis. DTW_I can warp the x-axis of a shake against the y-axis differently and produce a prototype whose channels no longer describe one motion; DTW_D keeps them locked. Shokoohi-Yekta et al. showed neither dominates and the choice is data-dependent, like the project's 'DTW or not depends on the data'. Failure addressed: the project has no multi-channel SOM at all; stacking channels into one long vector (the obvious Euclidean baseline) loses the shared time axis and the alignment.
ideas.why_pd: Single-channel today; becomes relevant with two microphones, or with the current pulse recorded alongside the acoustic one (DTW_D with the current channel as a timing anchor), or by feeding the series and its envelope or derivative as a second channel (a cheap way to fold idea 11 into DTW_D).
ideas.why_movement: The central ingredient for accelerometer + gyroscope gestures and activities; the whole movement goal rests on it.
ideas.control: The Euclidean SOM on the stacked, per-channel z-scaled channels; DTW_D vs DTW_I vs Euclidean, same seeds, same band (10%, 20%); a second control, the univariate DTW-SOM on the single best channel, shows the gain from more channels.
ideas.how_to_test: BasicMotions (80 series, 6 channels x 100 points, 4 classes) and UWaveGestureLibrary (440 series, 3 channels x 315 points, 8 classes), both from the UEA 2018 archive; sizes 3x3, 5x5, 7x7 for BasicMotions (small N) and 4x4, 7x7, 10x10 for UWave; 10 seeds. Read ARI, NMI, purity, TE, KL, TP (own distance), QE within one distance, used units, alignments (DTW_I = c x DTW_D), seconds, and a channel-consistency reading for prototypes (the lag between channels' paths under DTW_I). Win: D or I beats the stacked Euclidean SOM on ARI and TE on >= 7 of 10 seeds; report which of D/I wins per data set.
ideas.cost: DTW_D costs the univariate recursion with a c-term local cost; DTW_I costs c alignments; the data loader (ts/arff) is most of the work.
anchors: Shokoohi-Yekta, Hu, Jin, Wang & Keogh (2017) Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 31(1), 1-31 (verified)
Bagnall et al. (2018) arXiv:1811.00075: UEA multivariate archive; BasicMotions 6 x 100 x 4 classes, UWaveGestureLibrary 3 x 315 x 8 classes (verified)
Liu, Zhong, Wickramasuriya & Vasudevan (2009) Pervasive and Mobile Computing 5(6), 657-675: uWave (pages unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no: every series in the project is univariate (GesturePebbleZ1 and ShakeGestureWiimoteZ are the z-axis only).
ideas.risk: With 80 series BasicMotions cannot support a 10x10 map (use small maps and mind the QE/TE traps); channel scale dominates unless z-scaled per channel; DTW_I prototypes can look fine by QE and be physically meaningless.
ideas.expected_gain: large on movement compared with the only option the project has now (a stacked Euclidean vector); unknown between D and I.
ideas.problems: Not an improvement of the SOM but the missing input layer for the movement goal; fine, but say so. The PD motivation is decorative today (one microphone); 'series plus envelope as a second channel' changes the distance, it is not a multichannel case. BasicMotions has 80 series: a 7 x 7 map (49 units) is under two series per unit and the QE/TE traps bite; use 3 x 3 and 4 x 4 there or add a larger UEA set (Epilepsy, 275 series, 3 channels x 206, 4 classes, unverified). DTW_I prototypes can look fine by QE and be physically meaningless (admitted) and cost c alignments. Channel scale dominates unless z-scaled per channel over the whole data set (admitted).
ideas.corrections: Correctness check: DTW_D with band 0 must equal the stacked Euclidean SOM bit for bit (same summed local cost), which is the control. z-scale per channel over the data set, never per series. Read every map with its own distance AND with one common distance (the project's reading lesson from pd_acoustic). Keep the channel-lag diagnostic for DTW_I. Order of work: loader for the UEA .ts files, DTW_D, stacked control, then DTW_I. Shokoohi-Yekta et al. 2017 DMKD 31(1):1-31 verified; UEA archive counts (BasicMotions 6 x 100 x 4, UWaveGestureLibrary 3 x 315 x 8, 440 series) correct; Liu et al. 2009 Pervasive and Mobile Computing 5(6):657-675 plausible.

ideas.title: DTW step patterns and slope constraints: stop the pinch at the source
ideas.lens: distances and alignments inside the SOM
ideas.what_it_changes: The DTW recursion's allowed moves: instead of unconstrained symmetric steps (any run of horizontal or vertical moves inside the band), Sakoe-Chiba's symmetricP1 (at most one off-diagonal step between diagonal steps, local slope between 1/2 and 2), P05, P2, or Itakura's parallelogram. The update is the same along-path mean, but each prototype point now receives at most two series points, so no prototype point is pulled by a long run of samples.
ideas.mechanism: Pinching: with free runs one prototype point can absorb a whole ringing cycle and one series point can be spread over many prototype points; the prototype's events bunch and its tail is averaged from heterogeneous samples, which is what the project's re-timing, widening window and births from data repair afterwards. A slope limit prevents the pinch at the source: warping becomes a slow bounded speed change, and a 2:1 bound also limits how far a ringing cycle can be stretched (less frequency warping).
ideas.why_pd: Ringing cycles cannot be collapsed; jitter and slow decay-rate differences pass.
ideas.why_movement: A gesture rarely runs more than 2x faster or slower than another instance of itself: the slope bound is the physical prior for human motion.
ideas.control: The project's DTW-SOM (unconstrained symmetric2 step, same band, same seeds, same start and order); the DTW-SOM + re-timing as the project's fix for the symptom.
ideas.how_to_test: CBF (timing error exists there), pd_acoustic, Trace, GesturePebbleZ1, ShakeGestureWiimoteZ; sizes 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds; step pattern in {symmetric2 (control), symmetricP05, symmetricP1, symmetricP2, Itakura}. Judge QE in plain DTW for all (a constrained DTW is >= the unconstrained one, so its own QE is not comparable); TE, KL; ARI, NMI, purity; timing error of prototypes on CBF; cells and seconds; used units. Win: timing error and TE both lower on >= 7 of 10 seeds with ARI not lower. The dtw package's step patterns give a bit-for-bit reference for the distance.
ideas.cost: A few lines in the recursion (three candidate predecessors with weights); same O(L*w).
anchors: Sakoe & Chiba (1978) IEEE Trans. ASSP 26(1), 43-49: step patterns and slope constraints
Itakura (1975) IEEE Trans. ASSP 23(1), 67-72
Giorgino (2009) J. Stat. Software 31(7): the dtw package's step patterns
ideas.already_tested: no: the project repaired the timing after training (re-timing), with a widening window, or by growing; the step pattern was never changed.
ideas.risk: A slope bound plus a narrow band can leave no legal path for very different lengths (keep the band >= 10% and the different-lengths core's diagonal band); P2 is close to Euclidean on short series, so the gain may vanish on 125-point pulses; with a widening window the early phase is Euclidean under every pattern anyway.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on timing error and TE (the mechanism targets the pinch directly); small on ARI.
ideas.problems: The pinch is documented (longest run of copied points 1.0 -> 12.8 as the window widens; events bunch in the middle, timing error 4.4 vs 0.8), so the mechanism targets a measured symptom at its source, which is the kind of idea the project likes. But on 125-point pulses with a 12-sample band, symmetricP1/P2 is nearly the diagonal, so on PD this converges with L6 and the ARI gain is small (admitted); the real test is CBF, Trace and the gestures. With a slope bound AND a narrow band, the different-lengths sets may have no legal path. The symmetricP* patterns carry step weights (1, 2, 1), so the dtw package's normalised distance is not the project's unnormalised one; the along-path mean ignores the weights, which is fine but must be stated.
ideas.corrections: Verify the distance against dtw::dtw(..., step.pattern = symmetricP1)$distance (unnormalised) as the bit-for-bit reference. Keep symmetric2 + band as the control and add the widening window as the symptom-fix rival. Report the longest run of copied points per pattern as the direct reading of the mechanism, next to the CBF timing error. Run CBF, Trace and the gesture sets first, PD last. For the different-lengths sets keep the diagonal band at least as wide as the length ratio requires. Sakoe & Chiba 1978 IEEE Trans. ASSP 26(1):43-49, Itakura 1975 IEEE Trans. ASSP 23(1):67-72, Giorgino 2009 JSS 31(7) all correct.

ideas.title: Distances on transformed series: envelope, log-spectrum, cepstrum, scattering, and the physical (A, tau, f) summary
ideas.lens: distances and alignments inside the SOM
ideas.what_it_changes: The SOM trains on a transform of each series with the Euclidean step unchanged in that space: (a) the Hilbert envelope |x + iH(x)| (phase removed, decay kept); (b) the log-magnitude spectrum (shift-invariant, ringing frequency kept); (c) the real cepstrum (source pulse separated from resonance); (d) the wavelet scattering transform (shift-invariant, stable to small deformations, coarse time order kept); (e) a 3-coordinate physical summary from the PD pulse model x(t) ~ A exp(-t/tau) sin(2 pi f t + phi): (log A, tau, f). Prototypes are read back as envelopes or spectra, or, where there is no inverse (scattering), as the unit's medoid series. A two-view distance d = d_time(after one shift) + lambda*d_logspec combines (a)/(b) with idea 6.
ideas.mechanism: The invariances a PD pulse needs (shift, phase) go into the representation instead of into the alignment, so the SOM keeps its cheap, well-conditioned Euclidean update. The project's own hint: on pd_acoustic the Euclidean SOM read with DTW nearly matched the DTW-SOM, so the classes are nearly separable without elastic alignment once the right view is taken. Failure addressed: the Euclidean SOM is phase-sensitive (two identical pulses a quarter cycle apart look different) and the DTW-SOM warps frequency.
ideas.why_pd: Corona, void and air-gap discharges differ in ringing frequency (source geometry and microphone path resonance), decay time and loudness; noise is flat in spectrum: the log-spectrum and the envelope encode exactly these. The (log A, tau, f) map is a 3-D physically readable map and the strongest control for 'is anything beyond these three numbers being used?'.
ideas.why_movement: The log-spectrum loses the order of strokes (bad for gestures that differ in sequence); scattering keeps order up to its window; per-channel envelopes are a reasonable activity (not gesture) descriptor.
ideas.control: The Euclidean SOM on the raw asinh series and the DTW-SOM, same seeds; for each transform, the same transform under the plain SOM is the control for any alignment added on top of it.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic first, then BasicMotions with per-channel transforms; sizes 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds; one map per view: raw, envelope, log-spectrum (one-sided, 63 bins), cepstrum (first 20 quefrencies), scattering (order 2, J = 4, Q = 8; an R implementation may need a small C++ filter bank, availability unverified), the 3-parameter fit. Read ARI, NMI, purity, used units, TE, KL, TP within each view, QE only within a view; add two PD readings analogous to CBF's timing error: the prototype's ringing-frequency error and decay-time error against its class's median. Win: ARI above both controls on >= 7 of 10 seeds; the 3-parameter map's ARI says how much of the gain is the physics.
ideas.cost: One transform per series once (FFT); training is the cheapest kind; scattering is the only heavy transform and still far cheaper than DTW.
anchors: Anden & Mallat (2014) IEEE Trans. Signal Processing 62(16), 4114-4128: deep scattering spectrum
Mallat (2012) Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 65(10), 1331-1398: group invariant scattering
Bogert, Healy & Tukey (1963): the cepstrum (unverified)
Oppenheim & Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing: Hilbert envelope and real cepstrum
ideas.already_tested: partly: derivative DTW is one transform (slopes), no gain in general and a win on the solar I-V curves; no spectral, envelope, cepstral or scattering view, and no physical-parameter map, was tested.
ideas.risk: A 125-sample pulse gives a coarse spectrum (about 4 kHz per bin at 500 kS/s) and windowing effects; the physics fit fails on the noise class (tau undefined): treat a failed fit as its own flag; views cannot be compared by QE; the movement goal gains little from (b) and (c).
ideas.expected_gain: moderate to large on PD ARI (honest guess: log-spectrum or envelope plus loudness separates the three discharge types better than time-domain alignment); small on gestures; the 3-parameter control may be embarrassingly strong, which is a finding either way.
ideas.problems: (1) The physical fit x(t) ~ A exp(-t/tau) sin(2 pi f t + phi) assumes one damped sinusoid; airborne PD acoustics in an anechoic chamber are not that: corona gives a short broadband click (N-wave-like), the void discharge is heard through the insulator wall (low-passed, multi-modal structural ringing), so the fit is ill-posed for at least two classes and non-convex in f - it will fail on more than the noise class. (2) The Hilbert envelope removes phase but not shift; it is listed as if it were shift-invariant. (3) The scattering transform has no R implementation I know of (unverified) and is the heaviest item for a secondary gain. (4) A 63-bin spectrum at 4 kHz per bin from a rectangular 125-sample window leaks the loud onset across bins. (5) The two-view distance adds a lambda knob.
ideas.corrections: Replace the 3-parameter fit by a model-free 4-5 number descriptor map: log RMS, spectral centroid, spectral bandwidth, envelope decay time to 1/e of the peak, onset time. This is what acoustic PD pulse-shape classification uses in practice (unverified) and it cannot fail. Make it the strongest plain control for EVERY time-domain variant on pd_acoustic: if a 5-number SOM matches the DTW-SOM's ARI, the whole elastic family is moot for this data set, which is the single most useful number the researcher can get. Compute the spectrum after L6's shift and with a Hann window. First round: envelope map and log-spectrum map, each its own view; drop scattering and the cepstrum until those two are read. Keep the two PD readings (prototype ringing-frequency error and decay-time error against the class median) as the PD analogue of CBF's timing error. Anden & Mallat 2014 IEEE TSP 62(16):4114-4128 and Mallat 2012 CPAM 65(10):1331-1398 correct; Bogert, Healy & Tukey 1963 is the Proc. Symposium on Time Series Analysis cepstrum paper (plausible).

ideas.title: 1-D Wasserstein / EMD between normalised energy profiles or spectra: the transport view
ideas.lens: distances and alignments inside the SOM
ideas.what_it_changes: The distance between two series becomes the 1-D Wasserstein-2 distance between their normalised energy distributions over time (p_x(t) = x(t)^2 / sum x^2) or over frequency (normalised magnitude spectrum): W2 equals the L2 distance between quantile functions, O(L) after a cumulative sum. The SOM trains in quantile-function coordinates Q_x(u) on a fixed u grid, so the update is the Euclidean step on Q and the prototype is the exact 1-D Wasserstein barycentre, read back by inverting Q. Loudness is kept as the scalar coordinate of idea 3 with weight lambda.
ideas.mechanism: The physics (transport) view: moving a lump of energy later by dt costs mass x dt. Euclidean cost is blind to where a mismatch is (two non-overlapping peaks cost the same at any separation), DTW within the band charges nothing for a shift and then forbids it; W2 grows linearly and smoothly with the shift, and its barycentre MOVES peaks (displacement interpolation) rather than fading them in and out as the Euclidean mean does: the smeared-ramp failure of the Kohonen SOM prototypes on CBF becomes a moved ramp.
ideas.why_pd: The energy-over-time distribution is the decay profile (void slow, corona fast) plus the onset time, with phase removed; over frequency it is the ringing-frequency distribution; both are what differs between the discharge types.
ideas.why_movement: Per-channel energy distributions lose the sign (direction) of motion: a partial descriptor of activity intensity; better as a second term of a combined distance than alone.
ideas.control: The Euclidean SOM on the SAME normalised energy series (same transform, plain distance), which isolates the transport metric from the representation; plus the raw Euclidean SOM and the DTW-SOM; same seeds, same start and order.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic (time and frequency versions), CBF (shifted events: the mechanism check), Trace; sizes 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds; quantile grid of 64 and 128 points; lambda in {0, 0.3, 1}. Read ARI, NMI, purity, used units, TE, KL, TP (W2 and Euclidean), QE within one distance, timing error of the read-back prototypes on CBF, seconds (should be near the classic SOM's). Win: ARI and TE better than the same-transform Euclidean control on >= 7 of 10 seeds.
ideas.cost: A cumsum and an interpolation per series once; training is Euclidean on 64-128 coordinates, as cheap as the classic SOM.
anchors: Peyre & Cuturi (2019) Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 11(5-6): computational optimal transport, 1-D closed form and barycentres
Kolouri, Park, Thorpe, Slepcev & Rohde (2017) IEEE Signal Processing Magazine 34(4), 43-59: transport embeddings (unverified pages)
Rubner, Tomasi & Guibas (2000) IJCV 40(2), 99-121: EMD
Villani (2009) Optimal Transport: Old and New
ideas.already_tested: no.
ideas.risk: Normalisation discards loudness (keep lambda); the signed series must be turned into a non-negative density (energy, envelope or spectrum); quantile coordinates make a sharp onset a near-vertical segment that a coarse u grid blurs; on gestures the sign loss may cost more than transport gains.
ideas.expected_gain: unknown to moderate on PD; moderate on prototype readability and timing for shifted events (CBF); small on gestures.
ideas.problems: (1) On raw pressure the energy profile p^2 / sum p^2 of a loud pulse is a near-delta at the first cycle for every class (four decades of dynamic range), so the quantile functions are flat and all pulses look alike; on asinh^2 the profile is meaningful but is no longer 'energy'. (2) Sign is lost: the polarity of the first half-cycle (compression or rarefaction first) is a possible PD cue (unverified for this set). (3) The quantile grid blurs the onset (admitted). (4) The frequency version competes directly with L11's log-spectrum map and differs only in the metric; the loudness coordinate is L3's knob. (5) 'The physics (transport) view' is a label; the testable mechanism is 'shifted peaks cost linearly and the barycentre moves rather than fades', and CBF is the one honest test of it.
ideas.corrections: Define the density as the Hilbert envelope of the asinh series normalised to unit mass (or |asinh p|), never p^2. Keep the same-transform Euclidean control (Euclidean on the normalised envelope) and add a Euclidean SOM on the CDF, which separates 'quantile coordinates' from 'transport'. Run the CBF timing-error test first (moved ramp vs smeared ramp, read with the existing timing-error measure), PD second with the frequency version as a rival of L11's log-spectrum map. A PD precedent worth citing: cumulative-energy curves are what acoustic-emission and PD localisation use for arrival-time picking (AIC/Hinkley pickers, unverified), so the time version is a known PD object, not an import. Peyre & Cuturi 2019 FnT ML 11(5-6), Kolouri et al. 2017 IEEE SPM 34(4):43-59, Rubner et al. 2000 IJCV 40(2):99-121, Villani 2009 all correct.

ideas.title: Shape or loudness? Peak-normalise each pulse and carry log-peak as its own weighted channel
ideas.what_it_changes: The representation step only. Three arms: (a) shape only, x = p / max|p|; (b) shape plus one appended column lambda * log10(max|p| / 1 mPa) treated as a scalar channel (excluded from DTW warping, added as a squared difference in the distance and updated by the ordinary rule); (c) the current asinh(p / 1 mPa). Map, schedule and distance are unchanged.
ideas.mechanism: asinh(1e4) is about 9.9, so four decades of loudness become a feature of ~10 units against a shape range of a few units: the SOM may be sorting pulses by how loud they are, which separates the four lab sources but does not transfer (loudness in the field is distance, 1/r spreading and air absorption of roughly 1 dB/m at 40 kHz (unverified), not source type). Shape (rise, ringing, decay) travels better. Splitting the two tells which one the map uses, and the weighted channel lets the user dial loudness in by lambda. This addresses a failure the plain SOM cannot show from inside: a high ARI that is really a loudness meter.
ideas.why_pd: Direct: amplitude (apparent charge in electrical PD, pressure here) is the quantity of record but the worst feature for recognising a source at an unknown distance; the IEC 60270 practice is to report amplitude and classify by shape/phase (edition unverified).
ideas.why_movement: The same question for accelerometer gestures: magnitude (how hard) versus shape (which gesture); per-series normalisation and a magnitude channel also absorb sensor-gain differences between subjects and devices.
ideas.control: The current asinh pipeline (arm c), same map size, same seeds, same starting items and order; the project's z-normalised DTW arm (per-series standardisation, which also removes loudness) read first for PD.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic, 600 series; three representations x {online SOM, DTW-SOM 10%} x three hexagonal sizes (5x5, 7x7, 10x10) x 10 seeds, 20 passes. Read ARI/NMI/purity (shape-only vs asinh measures how much loudness carried), used units, TE/KL/TP within a representation; QE/EV only within a representation (they are not comparable across scalings). Then the transfer test: take held-out pulses (the unused 850 per class of the record, or a 100/50 split per class), multiply each by a random factor in [0.1, 10] to mimic distance, apply the representation, map onto the trained map and label by the unit's majority class; report per-class recall and false-alarm rate on noise before and after rescaling. Win: shape-only or shape + channel keeps recall within 5 points under rescaling while asinh drops, and ARI on the original data is not worse on 7 of 10 seeds at every size.
ideas.cost: Negligible: one extra column and a three-line change in the distance/update for the scalar channel.
anchors: IEC 60270 high-voltage test techniques, partial discharge measurements (edition unverified)
Somervuo & Kohonen (1999) feature sequences (in the project's references)
ideas.already_tested: partly: z-normalised DTW (per-series standardisation, which removes loudness) was in the benchmark and won clearly only on the solar I-V curves; its PD result should be read first. Shape + log-peak channel and the rescaling transfer test are new.
ideas.risk: If the lab sources differ mainly by loudness, shape-only ARI drops; that is the finding, not a failure. Peak-normalised noise pulses become amplified noise with random shape and spread over the map; the log-peak (or an SNR) channel restores them. lambda is a knob: test 0.5, 1, 2 in units of the series' standard deviation and report all three.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on transfer (recall under rescaling) and on trust; unknown on the original ARI, possibly a loss for shape-only, which is informative.
