ideas.problems: (1) The 'read first' step overstates what the project has: the benchmark's z-normalised DTW removed level and scale only inside the DTW alignment and winner choice; prototypes were averages of RAW values and the reading was on raw prototypes (summary Section 2, 'DTW aligns z-scores ... and the raw values are averaged'). So no shape-only pipeline exists in the project; the z-DTW PD result only says how the winner choice behaves without loudness. (2) The headline win criterion is a tautology for arm (a): x/max|x| is invariant to any positive rescaling by construction, so 'shape-only keeps recall within 5 points under rescaling while asinh drops' is guaranteed, not found. (3) The decisive control is missing: a loudness-only reading (1-D map or histogram on log10 peak alone, Ward k=4, same seeds). If loudness alone gives ARI near the waveform maps' ARI, every PD verdict in the benchmark was a loudness meter; without that number the experiment cannot say how much loudness carried. (4) Noise pulses peak-normalised become unit-peak random shapes that spread over the map; the false-alarm rate on rescaled noise (loud ambient noise) is where shape-only can lose badly, and the proposal measures it only as an afterthought.
ideas.corrections: Keep the three representations and the lambda sweep, but change the readings: (i) add the loudness-only control (log-peak alone) and report its ARI/NMI next to the others; (ii) for arm (a) the informative numbers are ARI/held-out recall on the ORIGINAL data (how much separation survives without loudness) and FAR on rescaled noise, not recall under rescaling; the rescaling test is informative only for asinh and for arm (b) at each lambda; (iii) state that z-DTW was alignment-only and is not a prior shape-only result; (iv) fold the held-out reading into PD8 (same pool, same majority-label rule) so this is one report section, and note the 850 unused pulses come from the same recording pool, i.e. same-session held-out, with rescaling as the only transfer proxy; (v) report the log-peak channel's share of the squared distance at each lambda so a reader can see whether lambda=2 simply re-creates asinh. IEC 60270 specifies apparent-charge measurement; 'classify by shape/phase' is PD practice, not the standard's text. Somervuo & Kohonen 1999 is in the project's references. The 40 kHz air-absorption figure (about 1 dB/m) is plausible from memory, unverified.

ideas.title: The PD engineer's baseline: Contin's T-W map and pulse-shape features as the input vector
ideas.what_it_changes: The representation: each pulse becomes 8-10 numbers: equivalent time length T (standard deviation of the normalised energy in time), equivalent bandwidth W (RMS frequency of the normalised energy spectrum) after Contin et al. (2002), rise time (10-90% of the envelope peak), decay time constant (envelope fit after the peak), dominant frequency and spectral centroid, log energy, log peak, crest factor, pre-trigger noise RMS; each standardised; Euclidean online SOM. Map, schedule and update unchanged.
ideas.mechanism: These features are invariant to timing jitter and (with peak and energy as separate columns) to loudness, and they are what PD practice uses to separate sources before any clustering. If a 10-feature map finds the classes as well as the 125-sample map, the waveform SOM is not earning its keep; if it does not, the user has a positive result for waveform maps. The T-W scatter itself, coloured by class, is the picture a PD audience trusts and belongs next to the map in the report.
ideas.why_pd: Direct: the T-W map is the standard source-separation tool of the PD community; it was built for exactly this (several sources, noise, one sensor).
ideas.why_movement: The analogue is a handful of segment features (duration, energy per axis, dominant frequency, zero-crossing rate) as the baseline every gesture-recognition paper reports before anything elastic.
ideas.control: Online SOM on the raw asinh waveform (same size, seeds, order); k-means on the features with as many centroids as units (best quantizer, no map); DTW-SOM on the raw waveform.
ideas.how_to_test: Compute the features in R (Hilbert envelope via FFT with zero-padding to 256 and a taper; T and W from the Contin formulas on the energy-normalised pulse). pd_acoustic, three sizes (5x5, 7x7, 10x10), 10 seeds. Read ARI/NMI/purity, used units, TE/KL/TP of the feature map (QE/EV not comparable across representations), seconds; plus the held-out per-class precision/recall and FAR with majority-label reading (PD8). Win for features: ARI higher on 7 of 10 seeds at every size; win for the waveform map: the reverse. Either outcome is a result; also report which features the units separate on (component planes).
ideas.cost: Trivial; 10-D vectors train about 12x faster than 125-D and need no alignments.
anchors: Contin, Cavallini, Montanari, Pasini & Puletti (2002) Digital detection and fuzzy classification of partial discharge signals, IEEE Trans. Dielectr. Electr. Insul. (existence verified; volume/pages unverified)
Vesanto & Alhoniemi (2000) two-level clustering (in the project's references)
ideas.already_tested: no: every PD map in the project was trained on the raw waveform.
ideas.risk: On a 250 us window the decay fit fails when the ringing outlasts the window, and the noise class gives random T and W; use robust estimators and keep the noise-RMS column so noise forms its own group. A feature map is a different animal from a time-series SOM and the researcher may prefer the waveform maps; it is still the necessary yardstick.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate to large on ARI/purity for the lab classes; the main value is as the yardstick every waveform variant must beat.
ideas.problems: (1) The feature vector includes log peak and log energy, so the feature-map vs asinh-waveform comparison is confounded with PD1's loudness question: a feature-map win could be loudness alone. (2) 'Pre-trigger noise RMS' assumes the 125-sample window contains a pre-onset segment; the reports only say the window is triggered by the current pulse (the acoustic arrival is delayed by about 29 us per cm of path), so that segment may not exist inside the stored 125 samples and the feature may need the record's full waveform. (3) An unsupervised ARI in a new feature space cannot be judged without a ceiling: nothing says whether ARI 0.6 is a poor map or an unseparable space. (4) The Contin T-W map was built for wideband electrical current pulses; on acoustic pulses dominated by the sensor's ringing, W will be nearly the sensor bandwidth for every PD class (the diagnostic PD4 proposes answers this and should run first). Otherwise the mechanism is sound and this is the yardstick the project lacks: if 10 numbers match the 125-sample map, the waveform SOM is not earning its keep.
ideas.corrections: Run the feature map twice, with and without the two loudness columns (log peak, log energy), and report both. Standardise features on the training 600 only and apply the same scaling to held-out pulses. Add a supervised ceiling per representation (cross-validated 1-NN or LDA accuracy on the features, and 1-NN with DTW on the waveforms) so ARI is read against what the space allows. Compute noise RMS from the noise class if no pre-trigger segment exists in the window. Run PD4's dominant-frequency/bandwidth-per-class table first; if W is the same for all PD classes, drop W and say so. Component planes are new to the project and worth adding as a reading. Contin, Cavallini, Montanari, Pasini & Puletti (2002), IEEE Trans. Dielectr. Electr. Insul. 9(3), 335-348 (volume/pages from memory). Vesanto & Alhoniemi (2000) is in the project's references. Design note: PD2 (second moments T, W of envelope and spectrum) is nested inside PD3 (full envelope and spectrum); run them as one nested experiment with shared controls.

ideas.title: Split the pulse into envelope and carrier: log-envelope plus log-magnitude spectrum as two Euclidean channels
ideas.what_it_changes: The representation: analytic signal via FFT (Hilbert), env(t) = |x + iHx|, log(env + eps) resampled to about 32 points; |X(f)| over the bins above the noise floor (16-32 bins), logged; the two channels scaled to unit variance and concatenated (weight per channel as a knob); plain Euclidean online SOM. For a DTW arm, DTW on the envelope channel only.
ideas.mechanism: An acoustic PD pulse is a slowly varying envelope (rise from the source, decay from source, path and microphone) times a carrier (ringing at the sensor's resonance plus source content). Two pulses with the same envelope but a few microseconds of carrier phase offset are far apart in Euclidean distance because their samples anti-correlate; that distance is noise to the classifier. DTW repairs it partly by warping at O(n w) cost and with the cycle-skipping risk. The envelope drops the carrier phase, the magnitude spectrum keeps the carrier frequency content without its phase; both are shift-tolerant, so a plain SOM with a small radius should match or beat DTW without alignments. This is also how ultrasonic PD detectors work: they demodulate to the envelope.
ideas.why_pd: Direct; envelope detection is the standard front end of airborne-ultrasound PD instruments.
ideas.why_movement: The same two channels per accelerometer axis (magnitude envelope and spectrum) are orientation- and phase-free, which is what gesture segments need when the window start jitters.
ideas.control: Online SOM on raw asinh; DTW-SOM on raw; and the project's strongest arm, the growing DTW-SOM; same sizes, seeds, order.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic, three sizes, 10 seeds. Read ARI/NMI/purity, TE/KL/TP/used within the representation, alignments and seconds (the Euclidean map needs none), held-out per-class precision/recall and FAR. Sweep the channel weight (envelope:spectrum = 2:1, 1:1, 1:2). Win: ARI at or above the DTW-SOM's on 7 of 10 seeds at every size at a tenth of the time; prototypes (envelope + spectrum) readable as rise/decay/frequency per unit.
ideas.cost: Small: preprocessing only; shorter vectors than the raw series.
anchors: Gabor (1946) theory of communication, analytic signal (unverified)
IEC TS 62478 acoustic and electromagnetic PD measurement (unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no.
ideas.risk: Edge effects of the Hilbert transform on 125 samples (zero-pad and taper); log of a near-zero envelope in the noise class blows up (set eps to the noise RMS). If classes differed in carrier phase relations (not physical) this would lose them. Spectral resolution on 125 samples is 4 kHz per bin.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on ARI with a large saving in time; unknown against the growing DTW-SOM.
ideas.problems: (1) The magnitude spectrum channel drops ALL timing including the onset delay after the trigger; in a lab with one source per class at a fixed microphone distance, that delay may be a class-specific feature (a leak), so the spectrum channel can lose ARI for a reason that has nothing to do with shape; the envelope channel keeps the delay, which muddles the attribution unless the two channels are also run alone. (2) The envelope resampled to about 32 points gives 8 us per point; a 10-90 % rise of a 40 kHz-band pulse is of that order, so rise information may be lost. (3) The channel weight is a knob (three values, acknowledged); the 'win' criterion ('ARI at or above the DTW-SOM on 7 of 10 seeds at a tenth of the time') is fine, but QE/EV must not appear in the comparison across representations (the proposal says so). (4) Overlap with PD2: T and W are exactly the second moments of these two channels. Mechanism (carrier-phase anti-correlation inflates Euclidean distance between pulses with equal envelopes; both channels are phase-free) is sound and matches the project's finding that DTW's PD gain is partly in the reading.
ideas.corrections: Add two single-channel arms (envelope only; spectrum only) so the reader sees which channel carries the ARI, and report the per-class onset-delay distribution as a zero-cost diagnostic to flag a timing leak. Use 64 envelope points, or keep the 125-sample log-envelope unresampled. Set eps to the noise-class RMS of the envelope, as proposed. Nest with PD2: features (T, W, ...) vs envelope+spectrum vs raw asinh waveform, same seeds, same controls, one table; QE/EV only within a representation, ARI/NMI/purity/used/TE/KL/TP across. Gabor (1946), J. IEE 93(III), 429-457, introduces the analytic signal (from memory). IEC TS 62478 (2016) covers electromagnetic and acoustic PD measurement (from memory).

ideas.title: Take the microphone out: whiten by the common pulse spectrum, or by the noise covariance, before comparing
ideas.what_it_changes: A linear transform before the SOM; the SOM is unchanged. Arm (a), sensor whitening: estimate the mean magnitude spectrum S(f) over all training pulses (or over corona, the most impulsive source) and divide each pulse's spectrum by max(S(f), floor), back to time (zero-phase Wiener-type filter). Arm (b), noise whitening: Sigma_n = shrinkage covariance of the 150 ambient-noise pulses (125 x 125); use d^2 = (x - w)' Sigma_n^-1 (x - w), implemented as the Euclidean SOM on Sigma_n^-1/2 x. Arm (c), the Manhattan rival: L1 winner with the matching sign (median) update, as a one-line plug-in.
ideas.mechanism: Every pulse carries the same sensor plus chamber impulse response, so the largest-variance directions of the data are the sensor's resonance, which says nothing about the source; Euclidean and DTW both spend their attention on it. Dividing it out makes the distance sensitive to the excitation, which is what differs between corona, air gap and void. Noise whitening is the matched-filter argument: measure distances in units of the noise so that frequencies where the ambient noise is loud count less. Both are routine PD measurement practice (sensor calibration, noise-adaptive filtering). A cheap decisive diagnostic comes first: the dominant frequency and -3 dB bandwidth per pulse by class; if all three PD classes peak at the same frequency, the ringing is the sensor and arm (a) should help; if they differ, the ringing is source information and only arm (b) should be tried.
ideas.why_pd: Direct: the acoustic chain (source, air path, microphone) colours every pulse the same way; PD practitioners calibrate it out.
ideas.why_movement: The analogue is removing the sensor's own response and gravity/orientation (high-pass, per-axis whitening by rest-period covariance) before comparing gestures.
ideas.control: Online SOM and DTW-SOM on unwhitened asinh data, same sizes, seeds, order; arm (c) L1 as the cheap robust-distance rival (expected wash after asinh).
ideas.how_to_test: First the diagnostic (one table: dominant frequency and bandwidth per class). Then whitening filters estimated on the training 600 (arm b on the noise class only); try whitening before asinh (on pascals, then asinh) and after, since asinh is nonlinear. Three sizes x 10 seeds. Read ARI/NMI/purity, TE/KL/TP within a representation, used units, held-out per-class precision/recall and FAR, and the spectral flatness of the prototypes before and after. Win: ARI up on 7 of 10 seeds and FAR down; a wash for L1 is the expected and reportable outcome.
ideas.cost: One 125 x 125 matrix multiply per item for arm (b); FFT filter per item for arm (a); L1 is free.
anchors: Wiener deconvolution (standard)
Mahalanobis (1936) (unverified)
Ledoit & Wolf (2004) shrinkage covariance (unverified)
Contin et al. (2002) on sensor-dependent pulse shapes (existence verified)
ideas.already_tested: no.
ideas.risk: Whitening amplifies bands where the microphone is deaf unless floored; 150 noise pulses for a 125 x 125 covariance needs shrinkage; the order whiten/asinh matters and both must be reported. If the diagnostic shows class-specific ringing, arm (a) would erase a real feature.
ideas.expected_gain: unknown; moderate if the diagnostic says the sensor dominates the variance; L1 expected wash.
ideas.problems: (1) Arm (b) as written is badly conditioned: a 125 x 125 covariance has 7,875 free parameters and the noise class gives 150 vectors; shrinkage papers over this. For stationary noise the covariance is Toeplitz (depends on lag only), so the right estimator is the noise autocorrelation or PSD from 150 x 125 = 18,750 samples into about 63 bins. Then Sigma_n^-1/2 is a spectral filter with 1/sqrt(PSD_noise), and arm (b) is the same operation as arm (a) with the noise spectrum in place of the mean pulse spectrum. (2) Whitening before asinh moves the scale, so the 1 mPa knee of asinh no longer sits at the noise level; the two orderings must re-set the knee or they compare different nonlinearities. (3) Arm (a) divides by a spectrum estimated from the same training pulses whose classes it then tries to separate; if classes differ in spectrum the mean spectrum is a class mixture and the division partly erases the differences (the diagnostic gate is the right guard, so this is a sequencing point, not a refutation). (4) Arm (c), L1: the sign update moves every coordinate by alpha*h regardless of distance, a different dynamic from the mean update; QE must be read in L1 and in L2 for every map, as the project reads Euclidean and DTW maps twice, or the comparison repeats the 'judge within one distance' trap. The expected wash is honest. (5) 'Spectral flatness of the prototypes' is a reasonable new measure but has no control value; report it for the raw maps too. Mechanism (sensor and chamber response colour every pulse identically; distance spends its attention on it) is physical, and the diagnostic-first design avoids adding a knob without reason.
ideas.corrections: Collapse arms (a) and (b) into one spectral whitening filter with two choices of spectrum (mean pulse spectrum; noise PSD via Welch over the 150 noise pulses), floored, zero-phase; drop the 125 x 125 covariance. After whitening set the asinh knee to the whitened noise RMS, and report whiten-then-asinh and asinh-then-whiten as two arms. Run the diagnostic table (dominant frequency, -3 dB bandwidth per class) first and publish it regardless; it is also PD2's and PD3's gate. For L1: sign update with the project's schedule, QE/EV/KL read in L1 and L2, same seeds and order; a wash is the reportable answer to the user's Manhattan question. Ledoit & Wolf (2004), J. Multivariate Analysis 88(2), 365-411 (from memory); Mahalanobis (1936) Proc. Natl. Inst. Sci. India 2, 49-55 (from memory).

ideas.title: Shift, don't warp: onset re-alignment once, or a lag-bounded cross-correlation distance, in place of DTW
ideas.what_it_changes: Distance and update. Arm (a), once before training: align each pulse by its onset (first crossing of 5x the pre-trigger noise RMS, or the envelope peak) with a fixed pre-onset margin, then the plain online SOM. Arm (b), per comparison: d(x, w) = min over |tau| <= L of ||shift(x, tau) - w|| with L = 2-3% of the length (3-4 samples, 6-8 us), or the normalised cross-correlation distance SBD of k-Shape; the update shifts x by the best lag and applies the ordinary rule (the same shift-then-update logic the project found essential for DTW: distance in the winner choice only hurts).
ideas.mechanism: For trigger-aligned PD pulses the residual timing jitter is a single delay (acoustic path length, trigger threshold), not a nonlinear warp. A 10% Sakoe-Chiba band is 12-13 samples = 24-26 us, about one ringing period if the carrier is near 40 kHz, so DTW can map one cycle onto the next and hide the ringing-frequency and decay differences that separate sources, and it bunches prototype events (the project's timing error). The project's own finding that the Euclidean map read with DTW nearly matched the DTW-SOM on PD says the shift is small and matters at the reading step; a shift-only distance should collect that gain at O(n L) instead of O(n w) and without warping artefacts.
ideas.why_pd: Direct: the trigger makes timing a shift problem; the carrier frequency is a feature to keep, not to warp away.
ideas.why_movement: Gestures have real nonlinear tempo variation, so DTW stays there; but segmentation jitter (where the window starts) is a shift, and the shift-only arm is the right control to see how much of DTW's gain on movement data is just that.
ideas.control: DTW-SOM at the project's 10% window; DTW-SOM at a 2-3% window (one-line change; the project showed the window is a property of the data); plain online SOM; all with the same sizes, seeds, order.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic, three sizes x 10 seeds. Read ARI/NMI/purity; QE/EV/KL judged in each map's own distance and, as the project did, every map also read with DTW; TE/TP; alignments and seconds; prototype timing (onset position of each prototype against its class mean) and the spectral peak of each prototype against its class. Win: ARI at or above the DTW-SOM on 7 of 10 seeds with fewer comparisons, and prototypes keep the class dominant frequency. Also report the first-look number: ARI of the existing window sweep at 5% on PD.
ideas.cost: Arm (a) zero; arm (b) 3-4 shifted Euclidean distances per comparison or an FFT cross-correlation, 3-4x cheaper than DTW at 10%.
anchors: Paparrizos & Gravano (2015) k-Shape, shape-based distance (verified)
Sakoe & Chiba (1978) (in the project's references)
ideas.already_tested: partly: a shape-based distance with one global shift is on the project's untested list; DTW windows 5-30% were swept on 3 seeds but the PD-specific reading at 5% has not been made; onset alignment was never done.
ideas.risk: The noise class has no onset: the detector returns garbage lags; give noise a zero shift (no crossing, no alignment) and treat 'no onset found' as a feature. If a source really differs by a nonlinear within-pulse effect (dispersive propagation in the insulator for the void), DTW keeps an edge.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on time and on prototype readability; small to moderate on ARI.
ideas.problems: (1) SBD of k-Shape is a normalised cross-correlation, so it is scale-invariant and removes loudness; mixing it into arm (b) confounds the shift question with PD1's loudness question. (2) The lag-bounded shift needs an edge rule (what fills the vacated samples, or whether the distance is taken over the overlap and rescaled); this is a small knob and must be stated. (3) Lab leak: if the three sources sit at different distances from the microphone, the acoustic arrival delay after the current trigger is class-specific; onset alignment (arm a) deletes that feature, so ARI may fall for a reason that is good for the field and bad for the lab score; without the per-class delay distribution the reader cannot tell. (4) The claim that a 10 % band lets DTW map one ringing cycle onto the next assumes a carrier near 40 kHz (period 25 us = 12.5 samples); the reports do not state the dominant frequency, so this must be measured (PD4's diagnostic) before the cycle-skipping story is asserted. Everything else is sound and well anchored in the project: the 5 % window on pd_acoustic exists in the cache (window sweep, 3 seeds, all eight series sets), 'shape-based distance with one global shift' is on the untested list, and the control (DTW-SOM at 2-3 %) is the minimal rival.
ideas.corrections: Split arm (b): (b1) lag-bounded Euclidean with the shift-then-update rule, (b2) SBD labelled as scale-free and compared with PD1's shape-only arm, not with the asinh maps. State the edge rule (edge replication, or overlap-only distance scaled by 125/overlap). Report the per-class onset-delay histogram and the per-prototype onset and spectral peak as new measures; read every map with its own distance, with DTW, and with the shift distance. Apply the same onset detector to held-out pulses (PD8), with zero shift for 'no onset found'. Paparrizos & Gravano (2015), SIGMOD, k-Shape and SBD: verified. Sakoe & Chiba (1978): in the project's references.

ideas.title: Detection as novelty: distance-to-map with per-unit thresholds, and the Kaski-Lagus path as a topology-aware second score
ideas.what_it_changes: Reading the map: a trained map becomes a detector. Score s1(x) = QE(x), the distance to the winner, with a per-unit threshold t_u = the 99th percentile of the training QE of unit u (class-conditional: each unit models its own spread). Score s2(x) = KL(x), distance to the winner plus the path along the map from winner to runner-up: an item whose two nearest units are far apart on the map sits between prototypes (ambiguous), which no QE threshold sees. Train on noise only (is there PD at all?) or on the three PD classes (is this a new source?).
ideas.mechanism: Distance-to-map is the standard one-class use of a SOM. The per-unit threshold matters here because the classes' spreads differ by decades even after asinh, so one global threshold sits wrong for every class. KL uses the lattice, which QE ignores: it is the one score where the SOM is more than a k-means codebook, and it addresses the plain SOM's blind spot that an item halfway between two classes gets a small QE.
ideas.why_pd: Detection is the first job in the field (PD or not?) and the false-alarm rate on noise is the number asset owners ask for; the record's unused 850 pulses per class give a real held-out pool.
ideas.why_movement: Unseen gesture or fall detection is novelty against the map of known activities; the same scores and the same controls apply.
ideas.control: (i) The PD engineer's default energy detector: peak or RMS above k x noise RMS; (ii) k-means with as many centroids as units, QE score (same codebook size, no topology); (iii) a single template (class mean, Euclidean distance); (iv) QE with one global threshold versus per-unit thresholds; (v) QE alone versus KL as the score.
ideas.how_to_test: Train on the 150 noise pulses (or the 450 PD pulses), three sizes x 10 seeds. Score held-out pulses: the unused 850 per class from the record, or a 100/50 split per class. Report ROC and AUC, precision/recall per class at the chosen threshold, FAR on noise at 95% PD recall and per-class recall at 1% FAR, next to the project's QE/TE/KL/TP/used of the training map. Win: AUC above the energy detector and above k-means on 7 of 10 seeds; KL beats QE as a score on the between-class pulses (those whose winner and runner-up carry different majority labels).
ideas.cost: Nothing at training; one mapping per test pulse, with the project's lower-bound pruning.
anchors: Kaski & Lagus (1996) (in the project's references)
SOM quantization-error anomaly detection, e.g. Hoglund, Hatonen & Sorvari (2000) mobile-network anomaly detection (unverified)
Marsland, Shapiro & Nehmzow (2002) grow-when-required network (unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no: the project has no detection measure.
ideas.risk: A map trained on noise alone collapses onto few units in asinh units and the per-unit thresholds rest on few samples. The energy detector may already be near-perfect on lab data where loudness differs by decades, so AUC saturates at 1 for everyone; then run the detection test on amplitude-rescaled held-out pulses (PD1) to make it honest. AUC on 150-sample classes is noisy: always with seeds.
ideas.expected_gain: large on the detection measures against the energy detector only after loudness is removed; otherwise a wash on AUC and a gain only on the class-conditional reading and on the between-class pulses (KL).
ideas.problems: (1) The KL score s2 does not do what is claimed. KL(x) = distance to the winner + the path along the map from winner to runner-up (metrics report Section 4a). On an ordered map where two classes abut, a pulse halfway between a corona and a void prototype has an ADJACENT winner and runner-up, so the path is one step and KL is small: KL flags folds, not class ambiguity. The project already minimises folds (growing maps), so s2 would flag almost nothing. The score for 'between two prototypes' is the margin d(x, runner-up) - d(x, winner) or their ratio, with a flag when the two units carry different majority labels. The win criterion 'KL beats QE on the between-class pulses' is therefore ill-posed. (2) Per-unit 99th percentiles rest on about 24 training items per unit on a 5 x 5 map and far fewer on big maps or small units; the 99th percentile of 24 values is the maximum, so the thresholds are noise. (3) The energy detector will saturate (AUC 1) on lab data where loudness differs by decades, which the proposal admits; the honest version depends on PD1's rescaling, so this cannot run alone. (4) Reference: Höglund, Hätönen & Sorvari (2000) is 'A computer host-based user anomaly detection system using the self-organizing map' (IJCNN 2000), not mobile-network anomaly detection; the mobile-network SOM work is Höglund's later work with Laiho and others. The per-unit distance-to-map idea itself is standard and the controls (energy detector, k-means codebook, single template, global vs per-unit threshold) are the right ones; the operating points (FAR at 95 % recall, recall at 1 % FAR) are what a PD report needs.
ideas.corrections: Replace s2 = KL with the margin score (d2 - d1, or d1/d2) plus the label-disagreement flag; keep KL only as the map-quality measure it is. Estimate per-unit thresholds with a parametric fit (log-normal or scaled chi-square of the unit's training distances) or as a per-unit scale times a global quantile, and report how many items each threshold rests on. Run detection on the original and on the rescaled held-out pulses (PD1), always with seeds. Share the held-out pool and the majority-label rule with PD8 and write the two as one 'held-out reading' section. Fix the Höglund attribution; Marsland, Shapiro & Nehmzow (2002), Neural Networks 15(8-9), 1041-1058 (from memory). Kaski & Lagus (1996) is in the project's references.

ideas.title: Read the map as a PD engineer would: held-out labelling with per-class precision/recall and FAR, and cut the map by the U-matrix instead of Ward with k = 4
ideas.what_it_changes: The reading step. (a) Label each unit by the majority class of its training items (or 'empty'), map held-out pulses, read the confusion matrix: per-class precision and recall, false-alarm rate on noise. (b) The number of groups: a watershed or threshold on the U-matrix (or the Ward cut at the largest dendrogram gap) rather than k = number of classes; report the number found and the ARI/NMI with found-k next to the present ARI with k = 4.
ideas.mechanism: ARI on the training items with k given is the laboratory's measure. The field measure is: of the pulses called 'void', how many were void; of the void pulses, how many were called void; how often noise is called PD. Giving k = 4 to Ward hides the question whether the map finds four groups at all; the U-matrix is what the SOM offers beyond k-means and the project has not used it as a measure. This is the reading the detection target needs and it may re-rank the variants.
ideas.why_pd: Direct: precision/recall per source and FAR on noise are the numbers a PD report is judged by; a train-set ARI is not.
ideas.why_movement: Gesture classification is always reported held-out per class (subject-independent splits); the same reading applies.
ideas.control: The current Ward-k reading on the training items, on the very same maps (no retraining).
ideas.how_to_test: For every map already in the benchmark cache (all variants, three sizes, 10 seeds): add the held-out confusion matrix from the record's unused pulses (or a 100/50 split), the found-k and the two ARIs. Report all project measures next to the new ones. This is a measure, not a variant; the decisive comparison is whether the variant rankings change when read held-out: if the growing DTW-SOM wins held-out precision/recall as it won QE/KL, the verdict stands; if not, the ranking was a training-set artefact.
ideas.cost: None: no retraining; one mapping per held-out pulse.
anchors: Ultsch & Siemon (1990) U-matrix (unverified)
Vesanto & Alhoniemi (2000) (in the project's references)
ideas.already_tested: no: all reads were on the training items with k given.
ideas.risk: Majority labels on 25-unit maps are coarse, hence the sizes; the U-matrix watershed has its own threshold (take it from the Ward gap and report the sensitivity). A 50/class held-out split makes precision/recall granular at 2%; prefer the record's 850 per class.
ideas.expected_gain: none on the maps themselves; large on the trust in every verdict.
ideas.problems: The weakest objections I could find: (1) the 850 unused pulses per class are from the same recording pool as the 150 training pulses (the benchmark drew 150 at random from 1000), so this is same-session held-out: it tests over-fitting of the map and of the Ward reading, not transfer to other sessions, sensors or distances; the proposal calls it 'the field measure', which overstates it. (2) 'Ward cut at the largest dendrogram gap' is a weak chooser of k and adds a threshold; the U-matrix watershed adds another. (3) Majority labels on 25 units with four classes are coarse and the tie/empty rules are unstated; held-out pulses that land on an empty unit have no label. (4) For movement data a random split is wrong; subject-independent splits are the standard. None of these refutes the idea: every ARI in the project is on the training items with k given (benchmark Limits: 'ARI and NMI rest on one choice'), no U-matrix was ever drawn, and this reading costs no retraining and may re-rank every variant.
ideas.corrections: Name it same-session held-out and pair it with PD1's rescaling as the transfer proxy. Instead of one found-k, report ARI(k) and NMI(k) for k = 2..8 per variant as a curve (zero cost) and the k at the peak; give the U-matrix watershed count with its threshold sensitivity as a second column. State the rules: empty unit = reject (report the reject rate), ties broken by the nearer prototype. Add per-unit held-out QE (feeds PD6's thresholds) and the confusion matrix per size. For DTW maps map held-out pulses with LB_Keogh pruning and count the alignments. For movement sets use leave-subjects-out splits. Ultsch & Siemon (1990), 'Kohonen's self organizing feature maps for exploratory data analysis', INNC-90 Paris, 305-308 (from memory). Vesanto & Alhoniemi (2000): in the project's references. Write PD6 and PD8 as one section: same maps, same pool, two readings (classification and detection).

ideas.title: fp32 vs fp64 vs MPFR: a falsification test, not a feature
ideas.what_it_changes: Nothing in the algorithm: the Rcpp loops templated on the scalar type (float, double, long double) plus an mpfr::mpreal arm for one small case.
ideas.mechanism: The measurement chain bounds the useful precision: a 16-24-bit ADC gives 5-7 decades, and asinh(p / 1 mPa) folds the four decades of loudness into values of a few units, where float32 already keeps about 7 significant digits. The online update w <- w + alpha h (x - w) is a contraction, so rounding errors do not accumulate, and the only thing precision can change is the winner at a near-tie, which the seeds (start and order) already randomise far more. No gain is expected; the value of the test is to close the question with numbers rather than with an argument.
ideas.why_pd: The four-decade dynamic range is the one PD-specific reason anyone would suspect precision; asinh removes it.
ideas.why_movement: Accelerometer data are 12-16-bit integers; the same argument holds more strongly.
ideas.control: The project's double build, same seeds, starts and order.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic and one more set, three sizes x 10 seeds. Count the training steps where float and double disagree on the winner; compare QE/EV/TE/KL/TP/ARI/NMI differences with the seed-to-seed spread; run MPFR (50 digits) on a 5x5 map for one seed only (slow) to confirm the double result to the printed digits. Prediction: disagreements in under 0.1% of steps and differences one to two orders below the seed spread. Win for precision: differences larger than the seed spread. Also report seconds: float32 with SIMD may be the actual gain.
ideas.cost: float arm faster (half the memory traffic); MPFR 100-1000x slower.
anchors: Higham (2002) Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms (unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no.
ideas.risk: None beyond the time spent; the only surprise would be a speed gain from float32.
ideas.expected_gain: none on quality; small on speed for float32.
ideas.problems: (1) The proposed count ('training steps where float and double disagree on the winner') is not a precision measure: after the first disagreement the two runs follow different trajectories and are different maps, so every later disagreement is trajectory divergence, not rounding. (2) Near-ties in the winner choice on this data are dominated by exact ties from integer ADC quantisation (the benchmark's C++ check runs on 'integer series full of ties'); asinh of quantised pressures keeps those ties, and there the tie-break rule (first index) decides, not precision; a naive count would blame float for what is a tie rule. (3) The SIMD speed claim needs care: the DTW recursion has a serial dependency along the band, so float32 helps the Euclidean loop and the memory traffic, not the DTW core; 'long double' is 80-bit on x86 and software 128-bit on ARM (very slow), so that arm's seconds are platform-specific. (4) The value is a null result the user asked for; the mechanism argument (contraction, asinh folds the dynamic range, seeds randomise more) is correct and the prediction is near-certain, so the experiment should be sized small. Higham (2002), Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, 2nd ed., SIAM: real from memory.
ideas.corrections: Use a shadow run: at every step compute the float winner but apply the double winner's update (one trajectory), and count disagreements split into exact ties and near-ties below 1e-6 relative; separately compare end-of-run QE/EV/TE/KL/TP/ARI/NMI of independent float and double runs against the seed spread (the ratio of precision difference to seed spread is the headline number). Run MPFR (50 digits, Rcpp mpreal, not Rmpfr in R) on one 5 x 5 seed and report agreement to printed digits. Report seconds for float32 and double on the Euclidean and the DTW loops separately and name the CPU. Keep it to pd_acoustic and one movement set, three sizes, 10 seeds; this closes the user's question with numbers at low cost.

ideas.title: Data-driven size: a growth-stop rule and idle-unit pruning in the growing DTW-SOM, then GHSOM children
ideas.what_it_changes: Three additions to the existing growing loop. (a) Stop: births now happen at even steps; instead allow a birth only while the running QE over the last pass still falls by more than epsilon per birth, or while the worst unit's accumulated error exceeds tau1 x the map's mean; growth stops when neither holds. (b) Prune: a unit whose decayed win counter stays below 1/K per pass for a full pass after growth is removed (its cell freed; the next birth goes there). (c) Hierarchy: after the stop, any unit whose mean QE exceeds tau2 x the map's mean gets a child map (7 units, grown by the same rule) trained on its own items only (Rauber et al. 2002). The final size is no longer set in advance.
ideas.mechanism: The project's growing map ends at the same K as the fixed map because the benchmark says so, and on the blobs it still left about 12 of 64 units without a point. Idle units cost an alignment every step and distort TE (their prototypes can be runner-ups). A stop rule ends growth when further births only split clusters (purity's trap); pruning returns wasted cells; children refine only where the fit is poor, so resolution follows the data's error rather than the lattice. GHSOM also yields a cluster count without a Ward cut: each leaf map's parent unit is a group.
ideas.why_pd: Four classes of very different spread in asinh space (noise tight, void discharges varied in ringing): a flat map over-resolves the noise and under-resolves the discharges; a child map on the discharge units works at the discharge scale, with its own centring. In the field the number of PD types is unknown, so a stopped or hierarchical map gives a count.
ideas.why_movement: Activity sets are unbalanced (walking >> falls); a child map for a rare but important class; a stop rule gives a different map size per subject without hand tuning.
ideas.control: The growing DTW-SOM with its final size set post hoc to the stopped map's used-unit count (same seed, same order), and the fixed DTW-SOM at that size; for the hierarchy, a flat map with the same TOTAL number of used leaf units, and the Ward cut at the leaf count. Because QE/EV/KL fall with units, every comparison is at matched used units.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic, the 7 benchmark series sets, the 2 gesture sets; start at 7 units, cap 100 (cap 400 on PD); tau1 in {0.2, 0.5, 0.8} chosen on seeds 11-15, tested on 1-10 (the tearing_heal protocol); 10 seeds. Read used/dead units, QE and EV at matched used units, TE/KL/TP per map (on tiny child maps TE near 0 is the known trap: report child TE next to child size), purity against the random line at that unit count, ARI/NMI with k found vs k oracle, alignments saved (the main expected gain), seconds. Win = at matched used units, QE and KL not worse on at least 7 of 10 seeds AND fewer alignments AND ARI with k found within 0.05 of the oracle k.
ideas.cost: Counters per unit; stop and prune are about 40 lines; the hierarchy is a recursion over the existing trainer (about 150 lines of R); runtime goes down (fewer units, earlier stop).
anchors: Rauber, Merkl & Dittenbach (2002) The growing hierarchical self-organizing map, IEEE Trans. Neural Networks (unverified)
Alahakoon, Halgamuge & Srinivasan (2000) GSOM with a spread factor (unverified)
Fritzke (1994) Growing cell structures, unit removal by low win rate (unverified)
Project tutorial 12l: window per unit, removing idle units, a stop rule listed as untested

ideas.risk: The taus will be tuned on one data set, as the growing defaults were tuned on CBF (the benchmark's Limits); a matched-size comparison may show that the stop rule only picks a smaller K and the fixed map at that K is as good (the PCA-start lesson: a way to shorten training, not to improve it); child maps with few items hit the TE-near-0 and purity traps; prune-then-birth at the same cell can oscillate.

ideas.problems: The prune threshold is mis-specified: 'win counter below 1/K per pass' is the AVERAGE share, so it would prune about half the units; it must be 'zero wins in a full pass' or below 0.1 x N/K. Refilling the pruned cell with 'the next birth' breaks the growing map's own rule that a birth sits next to its parent where the fit is worst; a unit born into a far hole has unrelated lattice neighbours, a fold by construction. The expected 'large gain on alignments' is bounded: the growing map already saves ~17%, and a stop below the benchmark's K changes the size, so every reading is at matched used units (the idea says so). Prune: a unit with zero wins over a full pass after growth has stopped; do not refill. Control: the growing DTW-SOM retrained at the stopped size (same seed, same order) and the fixed DTW-SOM at that size; read QE/EV/KL at matched used units, dead units, alignments, ARI with k found vs oracle. Keep the 'k unknown' framing: a stopped map that gives a size and a count without hand tuning is the practical PD result.

ideas.title: Heskes' winner: choose the unit whose whole neighbourhood fits the item
ideas.what_it_changes: One line in the winner search: instead of argmin_i d(x, m_i), take argmin_i sum_j h(r_ij) d(x, m_j), the neighbourhood-weighted sum at the current radius. The update is unchanged. With DTW every d(x, m_j) is already computed for the winner search, so the sum is free. After training, items are mapped with the plain nearest unit as now.
ideas.mechanism: Kohonen's online rule has no energy function for continuous data (Erwin, Obermayer & Schulten 1992); Heskes (1999) showed that with this winner the online SOM is a stochastic gradient descent on E = sum_x min_i sum_j h_ij d(x, m_j), which is the quantity KL and TE approximate: fit through the neighbourhood. A unit at a fold (close to x but with neighbours far from x) is not chosen, so folds get no reinforcement; as the radius shrinks to 0.5 the rule converges to the plain nearest unit, so QE is not sacrificed at the end. It changes the winner in some share of steps, as the chaotic units did, but by a bounded data-dependent rule that vanishes with the radius, not by a memory of the unit's past state.
ideas.why_pd: The PD map's folds happen where the loud and faint classes meet; a winner rule that penalises folds should keep the corona, air-gap and void regions contiguous, which is what the Ward cut needs.
ideas.why_movement: Same; and inside the growing DTW-SOM the floating per-unit radius is exactly the h(r_ij) this rule needs, so the two make a consistent pair.
ideas.control: The online SOM and the DTW-SOM unchanged (same seeds, same order); log the share of steps the Heskes winner differs from the nearest unit (the chaotic-units diagnostic) and how it falls with the radius; also the fixed map with the smooth radius schedule (TE 0.036 on CBF), since any order gain must beat a smoother plain schedule.
ideas.how_to_test: All 12 benchmark sets (Euclidean) and the 9 series sets (DTW), 5x5 / 7x7 / 10x10, 10 seeds; also inside the growing DTW-SOM. Read TE, KL, TP (the targets), QE and EV (must not rise beyond seed noise), purity, ARI/NMI, the 'winner not nearest' share, alignments (unchanged) and seconds. Win = TE and KL lower on at least 7 of 10 seeds on most sets with QE within seed noise; if QE rises as with CHAOSOM (order bought with fit) it is a wash, because the half-radius SOM already offers that trade.
ideas.cost: Zero extra alignments; a weighted sum over the neighbourhood per step (at most K multiplications); about 15 lines of C++.
anchors: Heskes (1999) Energy functions for self-organizing maps, in Oja & Kaski (eds) Kohonen Maps, Elsevier (unverified)
Erwin, Obermayer & Schulten (1992) Self-organizing maps: ordering, convergence properties and energy functions, Biological Cybernetics (unverified)
Project drafts README: an early Heskes run existed, no result kept
ideas.already_tested: no (an early draft run with no kept result; on the untested list)
ideas.risk: Lesson 4's shape: it must beat the plain rival that does the same job, here a plain SOM with a smaller or smoother radius schedule; if the gain is only in the wide-radius phase it is wiped out like the PCA start. With a bubble neighbourhood the rule degenerates, so use the Gaussian.
ideas.expected_gain: small to moderate on TE/KL; none on QE; cheap enough that even a wash earns a row in the table
ideas.problems: One load-bearing omission: Heskes' energy uses a neighbourhood function normalised over j for each i (sum_j h_ij = 1). Without that normalisation a rim unit (3-5 lattice neighbours) has fewer non-zero terms in sum_j h_ij d_j than an interior unit (6), so at wide radius the rim is FAVOURED, not folds penalised, and the winner share drifts to the rim: the opposite of the claim. Also the energy is on squared distances (||x - m||^2, and for DTW the cumulative squared path cost, which is the project's DTW before the square root), not on the plain distance the project reports as QE. The claim that the rule 'converges to the plain nearest unit' at the floor is only approximate: with the project's Gaussian at r = 0.5 a direct neighbour still carries weight 0.135, so the Heskes winner differs from the nearest unit for items near a cell border until the end; harmless because the final mapping is by nearest unit, but the 'winner not nearest' share will not reach 0. Reproducibility: the weighted sum over K terms has no exact ties in fp64 on real data, but the benchmark's integer-series-with-ties test can tie; fix the tie-break (lowest index) so R and C++ agree to the last bit as the project requires. Heskes (1999) confirmed: Kohonen Maps, Elsevier, pp. 303-315.
ideas.corrections: Use h_ij / sum_j h_ij per unit i and squared distances (DTW: the squared cumulative cost). Log the winner-not-nearest share per pass next to the chaotic units' share, and the share of steps the Heskes winner was a rim unit versus the nearest-unit rule. Controls as proposed; add the smooth-schedule fixed map (TE 0.036 on CBF) as the bar for any order gain. Zero extra alignments with DTW only if all K distances are kept per step, which the winner search already does.

ideas.title: LVQ fine-tuning after the map: move prototypes to the class boundary when labels exist
ideas.what_it_changes: A second training stage on the same prototypes after the unsupervised map: label each used unit by majority; then for each labelled item, LVQ1: the winner moves toward the item if the labels agree and away if not (with DTW, the same warped update with the sign flipped); OLVQ1 gives each unit its own rate; LVQ3 updates the two nearest when they straddle the boundary inside a window. The lattice is kept for the picture but not used in this stage. New pulses are classified by the nearest labelled prototype.
ideas.mechanism: The SOM places prototypes by density, smoothed by the neighbourhood, not by class boundary; the Ward cut then hopes the classes are density clusters. LVQ moves prototypes until the 1-NN decision border approximates the Bayes border (Kohonen 2001, ch. 6). The project measures ARI of an unsupervised cut, but for PD detection the job is supervised classification of new pulses, and LVQ is the SOM family's tool for it. It also fits the project's finding that part of DTW's gain is in reading the map: reading is classification, which is where labels help most.
ideas.why_pd: Labelled lab data exist (4 classes x 150); faint corona vs ambient noise is a boundary, not a density gap, and that is the detection problem; LVQ with DTW prototypes gives a detector that is a handful of readable waveforms.
ideas.why_movement: Gesture and activity labels always exist for training; subject-to-subject shift is handled by a few LVQ passes on the new subject's labelled samples (adaptation of a readable codebook).
ideas.control: (1) The same SOM prototypes labelled by majority without LVQ (1-NN on prototypes); (2) k-NN on the raw series with the same distance (DTW-1NN is the standard time-series baseline); (3) LVQ1 from a random start with the same number of prototypes, to show the SOM start matters. Held-out: 10 folds per seed, since LVQ needs a test split the project does not use yet.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic, GunPoint, ECG200, Trace, CBF, Synthetic Control, the gesture sets; 25 / 49 / 100 prototypes; 10 seeds x 10 folds; 5-20 LVQ passes, rate 0.03 -> 0. Read held-out accuracy and macro-F1 (new labelled measures), purity and ARI/NMI of the prototype labels, QE/EV (will rise a little), TE/KL/TP (will rise: the re-timing lesson, units moved one by one disagree with neighbours; quantify it), timing error on CBF, alignments. Win = held-out accuracy above control (1) on at least 7 of 10 seeds and within a few points of DTW-1NN with about 100x fewer alignments per new pulse.
ideas.cost: One extra stage of a few passes with winner search only (K alignments per item): about 10-25% of the SOM's cost; about 60 lines of C++ (sign flip and window rule).
anchors: Kohonen (2001) Self-Organizing Maps, 3rd ed., Springer, ch. 6 on LVQ1, LVQ2.1, LVQ3, OLVQ1 (unverified)
Sato & Yamada (1996) Generalized learning vector quantization, NIPS (unverified)
Somervuo & Kohonen (1999) Self-organizing maps and learning vector quantization for feature sequences, Neural Processing Letters (unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no (LVQ on the untested list)
ideas.risk: It damages the order the project values (TE up); LVQ2.1 diverges without the window; label noise (ambient-noise recordings that contain faint discharges) pushes prototypes the wrong way, so use LVQ3/OLVQ1 with a small rate; on data where DTW already hurts (solar I-V) LVQ cannot fix the distance. Gains in accuracy are not gains in the map: report them in a separate column and do not let them overwrite the unsupervised verdicts.
ideas.expected_gain: large on held-out classification (what LVQ is for); zero or negative on the map measures
ideas.problems: The cost claim is wrong for the lab set: DTW-1NN on 540 training pulses needs 540 alignments per new pulse, 25-100 prototypes need 25-100, so 5-20x fewer, not 100x; 100x holds only for N >= 10,000. LVQ1's 'away' update is unbounded: a prototype on the noise/faint-corona border can be pushed off the data and end with zero items (a new kind of dead unit); count prototypes that end with no items. The subject-adaptation claim for gestures needs subject IDs, which the UCR gesture sets do not ship. It damages the map measures and the idea says so; the key is that the project has no held-out split, so this is the first experiment that must introduce folds, and the fold draw must be the same across variants for the seed-by-seed rule. Label noise in 'ambient noise' recordings is a real risk for PD and argues for the windowed rules only. Anchors as I recall them are correct (Kohonen 2001 ch. 6; Sato & Yamada NIPS 8; Somervuo & Kohonen 1999 NPL 10, DTW-LVQ for sequences).
ideas.corrections: Use OLVQ1 or LVQ3 with a window, rate 0.03 -> 0, 5-20 passes; report prototypes with zero items after LVQ. Control (1) is the same SOM prototypes labelled by majority (zero cost); control (2) DTW-1NN on the training fold with the same window; control (3) LVQ from random prototypes. Fix the 10-fold draw per seed once and reuse it for every variant and size. Report held-out accuracy and macro-F1 in their own columns and the unsupervised measures after LVQ next to them, never merged. State the alignment ratio honestly as N_train / K per new pulse.

ideas.title: Median SOM and relational SOM: prototypes as real series, any dissimilarity, no warped averaging
ideas.what_it_changes: Compute the N x N dissimilarity matrix once (DTW with any point cost: squared, absolute/Manhattan, multi-channel dependent DTW, soft-DTW, shape-based). Median SOM (Kohonen & Somervuo 2002): every prototype is a data item; batch step: for each unit the new prototype is the item minimising sum_x h(r_{c(x), i}) D(x, item) over the items in its neighbourhood. Relational SOM (Hammer & Hasenfuss 2010; online version Olteanu & Villa-Vialaneix 2015): prototype i is a coefficient vector beta_i over items (sum = 1); the distance of item x to prototype i is (D beta_i)_x - 0.5 beta_i' D beta_i; the online update is beta_i += alpha h (e_x - beta_i). The training loop never touches a series again.
ideas.mechanism: The project's DTW-SOM averages warped series (Somervuo & Kohonen 1999); the prototype drifts in time and blurs, and the project had to re-time, widen the window or give birth from real series to get readable prototypes, finding that births from the data fixed most of the timing. A median SOM keeps every prototype a real series throughout, so timing and shape are real by construction; a relational SOM keeps prototypes as mixtures of real series without any warped average. Because the loop sees only the matrix, any dissimilarity plugs in with no new update rule, including ones that have no averaging at all (shape-based distance, soft-DTW, DTW on 3 channels with a Manhattan point cost).
ideas.why_pd: A prototype that is a real pulse can be played back and shown to an engineer. With N = 600 the matrix is about 180k alignments once, against about 1.2M for 20 passes x 600 items x 100 units in the online DTW-SOM: cheaper, and the matrix is reused for every map size, seed and variant, a large saving for seed-by-seed testing. A |a - b| (Manhattan) point cost inside DTW is robust to loud-pulse amplitude noise even after asinh.
ideas.why_movement: The strongest case: gestures are 3-6 channel series and the project has no multi-channel loop; with a matrix, multivariate DTW (dependent or independent) is just a different matrix, and the gesture sets' different lengths need no resampling.
ideas.control: The DTW-SOM and the growing DTW-SOM (same seeds) judged with the same DTW; the batch DTW-SOM (DBA) as the batch rival for the batch median SOM; k-medoids (PAM) on the same matrix as the quantization bound without a map; and, for the readable-prototype claim, the re-timed DTW-SOM.
ideas.how_to_test: pd_acoustic, the 7 benchmark series sets, the 2 gesture sets, plus one 3-axis gesture set (e.g. UCR UWaveGestureLibrary X/Y/Z combined; exact set unverified); 25 / 49 / 100 units; 10 seeds with the same start items. Read QE in DTW (a medoid's QE is at least a mean's: the known price), EV, TE, KL, TP, purity, ARI/NMI, timing error on CBF (the target), dead units, alignments counted as N(N-1)/2 once plus 0 during training, seconds. Win = timing error and TE/KL better than the DTW-SOM on at least 7 of 10 seeds with QE within about 5%; a second win is cost: the whole 10-seed x 3-size grid from one matrix.
ideas.cost: The matrix once, O(N^2 L w); training is O(N K) lookups per pass on the matrix; about 120 lines of R/C++; the relational SOM exists in the SOMbrero R package (CRAN) for a first check.
anchors: Kohonen & Somervuo (2002) How to make large self-organizing maps for nonvectorial data, Neural Networks 15 (unverified)
Hammer & Hasenfuss (2010) Topographic mapping of large dissimilarity data sets, Neural Computation 22 (unverified)
Olteanu & Villa-Vialaneix (2015) On-line relational and multiple relational SOM, Neurocomputing 147, 15-30 (verified)
SOMbrero R package on CRAN implements relational SOM (verified)
ideas.already_tested: no; partly related: births from the data (DTW medoid of the worse half) are a one-shot median step and were the ingredient that fixed timing
ideas.risk: A batch median SOM may inherit batch training's worse order (the project's batch lesson); medoid prototypes fit worse (QE up): lesson 3, fit vs order; relational prototypes with negative coefficients cannot be drawn as a series (show the nearest item instead); the matrix does not scale past 5-10k items, fine for PD lab sets, a problem for long activity streams (use a landmark subset).
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on timing error and readability; large on cost per experiment and on multi-channel reach; small or negative on QE
ideas.problems: DTW is not a metric and not Euclidean-embeddable, so the relational 'distance' (D beta)_x - 0.5 beta' D beta can be NEGATIVE for a non-Euclidean D (the pseudo-Euclidean case Hammer & Hasenfuss discuss); the winner rule still orders units, but QE/KL from such values are not comparable with the DTW maps', and the share of negative values must be reported. The negative-coefficient risk the idea names does not arise in the online update it proposes (beta stays on the simplex); the negativity is in the distance. Deployment cost cuts the other way for PD: a relational prototype needs D(x, all N items) = N alignments per new pulse (600, six times the DTW-SOM's 100); only the median SOM (prototypes are real series, K alignments) fits a detector. The timing-error win on CBF is by construction for a medoid, so it cannot be the decider; and median SOMs on small N assign the same item to several units, so collisions must be counted. The multi-channel claim overstates the project's data: GesturePebbleZ1 and ShakeGestureWiimoteZ are single-axis (Z); a 3-axis set must be added (UWaveGestureLibrary X/Y/Z are separate UCR sets of the same items, combinable). A batch median SOM inherits the batch order problem the project already found.
ideas.corrections: Prefer the online median SOM (and Olteanu & Villa-Vialaneix's online relational SOM only as a cross-check) with the project's schedule and 0.5 floor. Compute the N x N DTW matrix once per window with a symmetric band, store the upper triangle and read D[min(i,j), max(i,j)] so no rounding asymmetry enters; cache it and reuse it for every seed, size and variant (this is the real reproducibility win: every map then depends only on start and order). Judge on TE/KL/QE in plain DTW, collisions (units sharing an item), dead units, ARI; report negative relational distances as a share. Add PAM on the same matrix as the quantization bound (this also serves L2's missing control). Cost arithmetic (179,700 alignments once vs ~1.2M per online run at K = 100) is right.

ideas.title: Cluster extraction from the U*-matrix (distance x density) instead of Ward with k known
ideas.what_it_changes: Nothing in training. After training: U-height of a unit = mean DTW (or Euclidean) distance to its lattice neighbours (already computed for KL's paths); P-height = number of items within a Pareto radius of the prototype (density); U* = U scaled by the probability that the local density is low (Ultsch 2003); clusters = basins of a watershed / flood fill on the U* landscape (U*C, Ultsch 2005), merging basins whose separating wall is below a threshold; the number of clusters comes out of the landscape. Items join their winner's basin.
ideas.mechanism: The project's ARI/NMI rest on 'Ward cut into as many groups as there are classes' (the benchmark names this as a limit and Chainlink as its failure): Ward cuts by prototype distance alone, ignoring lattice and density, and needs k. The tearing SOM tried to find the walls DURING training by cutting long links and lost because cutting changed the pull. The U-matrix finds the same walls AFTER training with no effect on the pull, and the P-matrix adds what tearing never had: a wall counts only where few items sit (a gap), not where a cluster is merely wide. The project already saw that part of DTW's gain is in reading the map, so the reading step is where a cheap, large change in ARI is plausible. Chainlink's two interlocked rings are connected along the lattice and separated by a wall: Ward cannot find that, a flood fill can.
ideas.why_pd: In the field the number of discharge types is unknown and noise is a wide, dense class; a density-aware wall between noise and faint corona is the detection threshold, read off the map rather than set by hand; the k found versus the true k is itself a result.
ideas.why_movement: The number of gestures or activities is open-ended (an 'other' class); basins give a count and an unassigned set (items on walls) that a classifier can hand to a human.
ideas.control: (1) Ward with k = true classes (the project's oracle); (2) Ward with k chosen by a data criterion (silhouette on prototype distances, or the largest jump in the Ward merge heights), the fair rival since U*C also chooses k; (3) a density clustering on the items with DTW and no map (DBSCAN-style) to show the lattice adds something.
ideas.how_to_test: Every benchmark set including Chainlink (the named failure case), PD, gestures; 5x5, 7x7, 10x10 AND 20x20 where N >= 480 (PD, Synthetic Control, colours), because Ultsch's method is meant for large 'emergent' maps and may fail on small ones, which is part of the test; 10 seeds; the same cached trained maps as the benchmark. Read ARI, NMI, purity, number of clusters found vs true, share of items on walls; keep QE/EV/TE/KL/TP in the table (unchanged by construction). Win = ARI of U*C with k found at least that of Ward with k chosen by criterion on at least 7 of 10 seeds, and within 0.05 of oracle Ward on most sets; a specific prediction to check: Chainlink's ARI jumps.
ideas.cost: No alignments beyond the neighbour distances KL already computes plus the N x K distances already computed for the winners; about 100 lines of R; the R package Umatrix (CRAN) has the U*-matrix and watershed for a first check.
anchors: Ultsch (2003) U*-Matrix: a tool to visualize clusters in high dimensional data, technical report, Univ. Marburg (verified existence)
Ultsch (2005) U*C: self-organized clustering with emergent feature maps (verified existence)
Ultsch & Moerchen (2005) ESOM-Maps: tools for clustering, visualization and classification with Emergent SOM (verified existence)
Vesanto & Alhoniemi (2000) Clustering of the self-organizing map, IEEE Trans. Neural Networks, the project's two-level method (unverified)
R package Umatrix on CRAN (verified)
ideas.already_tested: no (the project uses Ward with k known; choosing the number of groups from the data is on the untested list); partly related: tearing's pieces vs Ward found the same clusters
ideas.risk: On 25-100 unit maps the landscape is too coarse for a watershed (one unit is one pixel); the Pareto radius and the merge threshold are knobs to set on seeds 11-15; on sets without density gaps (ECG200, Italy Power) it will over- or under-split and lose to oracle Ward, a fair outcome since the oracle knows k. Any ARI gain here says nothing about training and must be reported as a reading-step result (lesson 6).
ideas.expected_gain: moderate to large on ARI/NMI where classes are density-separated (PD noise vs discharge, Chainlink, gestures); zero on the training measures; large practical gain: k from the data
ideas.problems: Ultsch's U*C is built for emergent maps of thousands of units; on 25-100 units a watershed has 25-100 pixels and will mostly fail, so the realistic test is the 20x20 maps on pd_acoustic, Synthetic Control and colours (N >= 480), which the idea acknowledges. The Pareto radius for the P-matrix is defined from the distribution of pairwise ITEM distances (an N x N matrix or a sample), not from the N x K table; for DTW that is L8's matrix, so this idea quietly depends on L8 or on a sampled radius. Chainlink's predicted jump can fail for a reason unrelated to density: on a 10x10 map the lattice gap between the two rings is bridged by dead units whose intermediate prototypes form the wall, so the basins depend on how many dead units line the seam; report the dead-unit share along walls. Density weighting may add nothing on the project's clean lab sets, so a plain U-matrix flood fill is the needed extra rival. Reproducibility: watershed basins depend on tie-breaking of equal heights (common with DTW on integer series) and on the merge threshold; the flood order must be fixed (height, then unit index). Umatrix on CRAN confirmed (v4.0.2, Umatrix/Pmatrix/UStarMatrix functions; authors include Thrun and Ultsch); Ultsch (2005) U*C is already in the benchmark's own reference list. It is a reading-step result only and must be labelled so (lesson 6).
ideas.corrections: Four columns per cached map: Ward with oracle k, Ward with k by a criterion (silhouette on prototype distances or the largest merge-height jump), basins of the plain U-matrix, basins of U*; plus DBSCAN-style clustering on the items as the no-map rival. Run on 20x20 first; include the small maps only to document where it breaks. Pareto radius from the 18-20% quantile of pairwise item distances per Ultsch (from L8's matrix for DTW, or a 2,000-pair sample); merge threshold swept on seeds 11-15. Report k found vs true, share of items on walls, dead units on walls, and the deterministic flood order used. Keep QE/EV/TE/KL/TP in the table unchanged.

ideas.title: Online ordering, then batch (DBA) convergence with the 0.5 radius floor kept
ideas.what_it_changes: The first 60% of the schedule runs the existing online loop (radius wide -> 1); the last 40% runs the existing batch loop (DBA for DTW) with the radius held at the online map's floor of 0.5 (winner plus a weak pull on neighbours), not shrunk to 0 as the benchmark's batch maps did. One switch in the driver; both loops exist already.
ideas.mechanism: The project found batch = best fit but worse order, and said why: its last passes with a small radius are almost k-means, and the batch maps skip the 0.5 rule so their radius shrinks to about 0. Online = better order because the ordering phase is a noisy stochastic descent. So the two are good at different phases: online for ordering, where the stochastic path matters, and batch for convergence, where the exact neighbourhood mean lowers QE with no order left to gain. Keeping the 0.5 floor in the batch phase is the fair test of whether batch's disorder came from the floor or from the batch.
ideas.why_pd: PD prototypes need the best fit inside the loud classes, where ringing and decay are small details after asinh (batch DBA gives it), and an ordered, readable map for the engineer (online gives it).
ideas.why_movement: DBA means of warped gestures are the standard readable gesture prototype; the hybrid gets them on an ordered lattice.
ideas.control: (1) The online DTW-SOM unchanged; (2) the batch DTW-SOM unchanged (radius -> 0); (3) the batch DTW-SOM with the 0.5 floor for the whole run, the control that separates the floor from the hybrid; same seeds, order and start; same number of comparisons (a batch pass sees every item once).
ideas.how_to_test: All 12 benchmark sets (Euclidean) and the 9 series sets (DTW), 3 sizes, 10 seeds; switch point 40 / 60 / 80% swept on seeds 11-15. Read QE and EV (fit target), TE, KL, TP (must stay at the online map's level), purity, ARI/NMI, timing error on CBF (DBA keeps timing), dead units, alignments, seconds. Win = QE at the batch map's level AND TE/KL at the online map's level on at least 7 of 10 seeds; if control (3) alone does the same, the finding is 'the floor, not the hybrid', and that is the result to report.
ideas.cost: No new code beyond the driver; same alignments; the batch phase parallelises over units.

Petitjean, Ketterlin & Gancarski (2011) A global averaging method for dynamic time warping (DBA), Pattern Recognition (unverified)
Project benchmark Section 10: batch = best fit, worse order; batch maps skip the 0.5 rule
ideas.already_tested: partly: online and batch each alone; the 0.5 floor only on online maps; the hybrid and the floored batch: no
ideas.risk: The PCA-start lesson: whatever the early phase does, the late phase can wipe out; at radius 0.5 the batch phase keeps a neighbourhood so the order should survive, but if the floor is too weak the last passes become k-means again (lesson 3); DBA's known timing drift of prototypes over many passes.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on QE with order kept, which is the whole point; small on ARI
ideas.problems: The most likely outcome is already predictable and the idea names it: control (3), batch with the 0.5 floor throughout, is in effect the SOM Toolbox batch default (fine-tuning radius ends at 1, not 0), which is known to stay ordered; the finding will probably be 'the floor, not the hybrid'. That is still worth a table because it converts the project's batch verdict from 'worse order' to 'worse order because kohonen's batch mode shrinks the radius to 0'. Two specification slips: at 60% of a linear schedule from r0 to 0 the radius is 0.4 r0 (about 1.2-2 on these maps), not 1, so the online phase should run until the radius reaches 1 (a share 1 - 1/r0 of the schedule); and at the project's Gaussian floor r = 0.5 a direct neighbour carries weight 0.135 and a 2-step unit 3e-4, so the batch phase is 'k-means with a 13% tether', which may be too weak: the metrics report's end-radius sweep puts the KL minimum around 0.5-1, so the floor must be swept. Cost accounting: a DBA step realigns every item to the new mean at each inner iteration, so the batch phase's alignments exceed one online pass unless DBA is capped at one iteration per pass; count them. The benchmark's batch maps used a PCA start; the hybrid starts from the online map, so all controls must share the seed's random start. Reproducibility (my lens): batch means are sums over many items; accumulate in a fixed item order per unit (parallelise over units, not items) or the result is not bit-identical across thread counts, and the project's 'same map to the last bit' standard applies to the hybrid too.
ideas.corrections: Switch when the radius reaches 1 (sweep 40/60/80% only as a secondary axis); sweep the batch floor over {0.5, 0.75, 1}; cap DBA at one iteration per pass and report alignments; random start for all four maps; parallelise the batch phase over units with a fixed item order. Read QE/EV against the batch map, TE/KL/TP against the online map, timing error on CBF, dead units. If control (3) matches the hybrid, report 'the floor' as the result and drop the hybrid.

ideas.title: Independent vs dependent multi-channel DTW, with an adaptive choice
ideas.lens: movement / gesture / HAR from wearable sensors
ideas.what_it_changes: The distance and the warp step for nch > 1. Dependent DTW (the demonstrator's only form) uses one path for all channels with local cost = sum over channels of squared differences. Independent DTW runs one DP table per channel, sums the nch costs, and warps each channel along its own path before the update. The adaptive form computes both to the candidate units and uses the independent cost for an item when DTW_I/DTW_D falls below a threshold set by a short unsupervised sweep.
ideas.mechanism: In a gesture the three axes are one rigid motion: when the wrist slows, all axes slow together, so one shared path is right and the independent form over-fits by letting one axis warp against noise. When channels come from different sensors (accelerometer and gyroscope with different latencies, two wrists in Cricket) one shared path forces a compromise and the independent form fits better. The plain map cannot tell which case it is in; the failure it addresses is a prototype smeared across channels that warp differently.
ideas.why_pd: Not for the airborne-ultrasound set as recorded (one microphone, one channel). It becomes the right question as soon as a second channel is added, e.g. the current pulse next to the acoustic one, or two microphones for localisation: those channels have different propagation delays, which is the independent case.
ideas.why_movement: Multi-axis sensors are the norm, and the project's gesture sets were the Z-axis-only UCR cuts, so the question has never been asked here. AllGestureWiimoteX/Y/Z cannot be stacked (instances shuffled per axis); use UWaveGestureLibrary (UEA, 3 synchronised axes), Cricket (6 channels) and the synthetic 3-axis gestures.
ideas.control: The dependent DTW-SOM (one path for all channels) with the same seed, start, order and band; and the per-channel Euclidean SOM. Judge within the DTW family with each map's own distance and with both DTW_I and DTW_D.
ideas.how_to_test: Data: synthetic gestures (nch = 3) in two versions, (a) one speed profile shared by the channels as now, (b) each channel's speed profile shifted by a random +/-5% of L; UWaveGestureLibrary (3 axes); Cricket (6 channels, subsampled to 200 points). Maps 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds. Read ARI/NMI/purity (own distance), QE judged with DTW_D and with DTW_I, TE/KL (own), used units, alignments (independent = nch tables) and seconds. Win: ARI higher on at least 8 of 10 seeds on (b) and Cricket, and not lower on 8 of 10 on (a) and UWave; the adaptive form within 0.02 ARI of the better of the two on 8 of 10 seeds everywhere.
ideas.cost: Independent: nch DP tables per comparison (3x for three axes); adaptive: both forms, about 2x. Implementation: a loop over channels around the existing DP and a per-channel warp; small.
anchors: Shokoohi-Yekta, Hu, Jin, Wang & Keogh (2017), Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, 'Generalizing DTW to the multi-dimensional case requires an adaptive approach'
ten Holt, Reinders & Hendriks (2007), 'Multi-dimensional dynamic time warping for gesture recognition' (unverified)
ideas.already_tested: no: every DTW map in the project was single-channel, and the demonstrator implements only the dependent form
ideas.risk: On rigid single-sensor gestures the independent form is a wash or worse at 3x the cost (the paper itself finds neither form dominant); the adaptive threshold needs a sweep, and the project's lesson 2 says the data decide more than the variant, so the gain may be a data property rather than a map improvement.
ideas.expected_gain: moderate on ARI where channels are not synchronous (two-sensor rigs); small or none on a single 3-axis accelerometer; unknown on TE/KL
ideas.problems: The adaptive arm is unsound in an unsupervised map. In Shokoohi-Yekta et al. the DTW_I/DTW_D threshold is chosen by training-set accuracy with labels; here there are none. Worse, DTW_I <= DTW_D always (the shared path is a feasible path for every channel), so the ratio is <= 1 for every pair and carries no signal that separates 'channels warp together' from 'the item fits this prototype badly'. Second, the independent form in the UPDATE warps each channel of the item along its own path, so the prototype's channels desynchronise over training and the prototype stops being a coherent multichannel series (the readable-template property the researcher cares about). Third, the paper's own result is that neither form dominates and the differences are usually small, so 'moderate gain' is optimistic. The claim that AllGestureWiimoteX/Y/Z instances are shuffled per axis is unverified. Not already tested: the project's maps were single-channel; this session's demonstrator implements only the dependent form, as the idea says.
ideas.corrections: Drop the adaptive arm, or pick per data set by an unsupervised score that is comparable across the two forms (KL or TE judged with ONE common distance), never by a ratio threshold. Run DTW_D vs DTW_I as two maps, same seed/start/order/band, on synthetic (a)/(b) and UWave/Cricket. Add a prototype inter-channel desynchronisation measure (mean per-position path offset between channels) for the independent map, and judge QE with both DTW_D and DTW_I as proposed. Also add the trivial control the idea omits: Euclidean on the stacked channels. References: Shokoohi-Yekta, Hu, Jin, Wang & Keogh (2017) DMKD 31(1):1-31, verified; ten Holt, Reinders & Hendriks (2007) ASCI conference, plausible.

ideas.title: Orientation-invariant channels: magnitude and a gravity-aligned frame, crossed with amplitude normalisation
ideas.lens: movement / gesture / HAR from wearable sensors
ideas.what_it_changes: A preprocessing map from the 3 raw axes to the channels the SOM sees, no change to the loop: (i) raw axes (control); (ii) |a| only, 1 channel; (iii) gravity frame: rotate each gesture so its mean acceleration vector points to +z, then use (a_vertical, |a_horizontal|), 2 channels; (iv) raw axes plus |a| as a fourth channel. Crossed with amplitude handling: per-gesture z-score, global per-channel scale, or none.
ideas.mechanism: A sensor is never held the same way twice; a rotation moves energy between axes, so the plain map must spend units on orientations of the same gesture, splitting a class across units (purity can look fine while ARI falls because the Ward cut joins the wrong units). |a| is exactly invariant under any rotation; the gravity frame keeps vertical vs horizontal (2 degrees of freedom) and removes only the yaw, which is where holding varies most. The price: |a| loses chirality (a left circle equals a right circle).
ideas.why_pd: No rotation to remove, but the amplitude arm is the PD question in disguise: loudness is a class cue there (corona quiet, air gap loud, four decades, hence asinh) and must be kept, while for gestures it should mostly be dropped. Run the same normalisation matrix on pd_acoustic and expect the opposite winner; that contrast is the result.
ideas.why_movement: Central: the Wiimote sets were recorded with the device held at varying orientations, and orientation is the first nuisance any HAR pipeline removes.
ideas.control: The 3-axis map on the same items and seeds; for the amplitude arm, the raw-amplitude map.
ideas.how_to_test: Synthetic gestures with rotation_deg = 0, 15, 45, 90 and a mirrored pair added (left circle vs right circle = flip of x); UWaveGestureLibrary; pd_acoustic for the amplitude arm. Maps 4x4, 7x7, 10x10; 10 seeds; Euclidean and DTW families.
